7	# 德国历史主义传统（前言·导论）

9	## 前言
10	
11	这部著作是对“传统历史主义”（“the old historicism”）的再检视，经典历史主义传统在德国肇始于18世纪中叶的克拉德尼乌斯，而终结于20世纪初的马克斯 · 韦伯。这一传统在超乎寻常的程度上塑造了我们的思想领域，因而我们如今在思维方式上都是历史主义者。不过我们面临着遗忘这一传统并使其消失在过去迷雾中的危险。当人们今天想起历史主义的时候，他们很可能意指文学研究中的“新历史主义”或者由波普尔在20世纪40年代所贬低的“历史决定论”。但这两者与古老的传统并没有太多共同之处。
12	
13	我主要的任务就是向英语世界的读者介绍历史主义传统的主要代表人物。我试图评估他们的历史重要性，分析他们的主要论证，以及指明关于他们思想阐释中的主要问题。我的方式兼具历史性与系统性： 历史性在于我把每位思想家置于语境之中，并追踪他的思想的演变；而系统性在于我评估其论证的有效性，并重构其思想的逻辑结构。
14	
15	我的终极期望在于这项研究能够拓展我们的历史视野。这里所研究的大多数思想家不为英语世界所熟知。有些人是第一次得到介绍，而另一些人则是第一次受到深入的检视。赫尔德、兰克以及韦伯的著作更为英语世界的读者所熟知，而他们关于历史的思想得到哲学家们的充分理解。
16	
17	某些原稿的读者对于缺乏政治语境的聚焦表示遗憾。我完全同意他们关于那种语境重要性的信念；但我认为这种研究必须建立在更为基础的说明与阐释的任务之上，而目前对多数思想家的基础研究尚未完成。我们只有在理解思想家写了什么之后才能理解他为何这样写。出于这个理由，有关他政治动机的研究必须植根于他主要观念的哲学阐释之上。其他读者对缺少引用历史主义的非德语材料表示不解。如果他们在这里没有获得充分预期的成果，那部分是因为篇幅的限制，部分是因为德语材料较之法语、英语或意大利语材料远远不为人所知。
18	
19	这部著作的主要先例与典范是弗里德里希 · 梅尼克的《历史主义的兴起》。梅尼克的宏大志向是追踪德国历史主义的起源，它的跨度从17世纪末这一传统的开端一直到以兰克为代表的传统的顶峰。然而，这也是梅尼克在500页后仍未超越歌德的原因。尽管梅尼克的著作具有重大的教益——他的文本分析具有可靠的洞察力，并且他的历史视角同时具备深度与广度——但它仍然有着严重的缺陷，从而难以作为合格的入门指南。梅尼克忽视了关键的人物，他的阐释通常会误置时代，并且他的概念图式具有误导性与简单化的特征。当前的著作试图根据后来的研究重述梅尼克的故事。
20	
21	这本书诞生的契机是2005年迈克尔 · 罗森以及布莱恩 · 莱特邀请我为《牛津欧陆哲学手册》撰写关于历史主义的文章。我之前长期研究默泽尔、赫尔德与黑格尔，因而相信自己有充分的资格来撰写这篇文章。进一步的研究很快纠正了我的幻想。如今在那卷著作出版若干年之后，我认为自己终于可以证明编辑给予我的信任。当前的导论就是意在弥补之前文章中的瑕疵。

31	### 1. 一种思想革命
32	
33	## 导论
34	
35	### 历史主义的概念与语境
36	
37	Friedrich Meinecke, Die Entstehung des Historismus, in Werke, eds. Hans Herzfeld, Carl Hinrichs and Walther Hofer (Munich: Oldenbourg, 1965), III, 1.
38	
39	1936年，梅尼克在他的权威著作《历史主义的兴起》序言中怀旧地写道，历史主义“是西方思潮所经历的最伟大的思想革命之一”。  梅尼克认为，历史主义之所以是一次思想革命，原因就在于它取代了之前非历史的思维方式。非历史的思维方式占据了自古典到整个中世纪的漫长历程，全新的历史思维方式则发端于18世纪中期。旧的非历史思维方式把人的本质、道德性以及理性视作绝对的、永恒的和普遍的；而新的历史思维方式则把它们看作相对的、变化的和特殊的。历史主义在决定价值、信念和行动的历史原因与语境的过程中，已经显示了它们如何依赖于这样的原因与语境的特性。因此，任何试图将价值和信念超越时代局限而普遍化的努力—仿佛它们能适用于全人类或普遍理性—都注定是徒劳的。任何有关普遍世界观、超自然启示、绝对道德准则、自然法或者自然宗教的信仰都是种族中心主义的体现，产生于突破个人自身时代限制的虚幻尝试。
40	
41	尽管梅尼克在今天已经失去学界的青睐，但很少有学者会质疑他有关历史主义重要性的论题。但假如我们接受了那种论题，那么有些解释性工作将摆在面前。我们必须回答这些非常基本的问题。历史主义更准确地说是什么？哪些人是所谓历史主义者？他们的中心目标与观念是什么？以及他们如何为自己新的历史化思维方式进行论证？
42	
43	关于这个术语的历史有着许多有用的材料。参见Dwight Lees and Robert Beck, “The Meaning of ‘Historicism’ ” , American Historical Review 59 (1953—1954), pp.568—577; Gunter Scholtz, “Historizismus” , in Historisches Wörterbuch der Philosophie (Stuttgart: Schwabe & Co., 1974), III, 1141—1147; Christopher Thornhill, “Historicism” , in the Routledge Encyclopedia of Philosophy (London: Routledge, 1998), IV, 443—446; Georg Iggers, “Historicism” , in Dictionary of the History of Ideas (New York: Scribner, 1973), II, 456—464; Erich Rothacker, “Historismus” , in Schmollers Jahrbuch 62 (1938), 3883—3899; and by the same author “Das Wort ‘Historismus’ ” , Zeitschrift für deutsche Wortforschung 16 (1960), 3—6。卡尔 · 波普尔在第一种意义上使用该术语。参见The Poverty of Historicism (London: Routledge, 1961), p.3。波普尔的用法在英语世界中尤为普遍。例如，参见Simon Blackburn, The Oxford Dictionary of Philosophy (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1996), p.174。而梅尼克尤其是在第二种意义上使用该词。参见Die Entstehung des Historismus, pp.1—10。
44	
45	任何定义“历史主义”的尝试都会立刻遭遇巨大的障碍： 这个词蕴含了太多的意义。这个术语曾被以差异巨大，甚至相互冲突的方式使用着。  对某些人来说，它意味着对决定历史普遍法则的尝试；对另一些人来说，它的意义正好相反： 标志着对那些法则的拒斥，以及尝试了解历史上独特的、单一的事件与个性。  哪种用法是正确的？我们当然不可能得出结论。我们不能把这一术语实体化，好像历史主义还有某种隐藏的本质以及更深层的核心意义似的，能够在它充满分歧与矛盾的使用中以某种方式持存。
46	
47	为了能够避免这一障碍，我将给予“历史主义”一种更具规范性质而非描述性质的定义。描述性的定义试图界定一个词意味着什么以及如何得到应用，而规范性的定义强调这个词应该意味着什么以及应当如何应用。规范性定义的唯一根据便是它有助于探询问题。既然我们在这里的兴趣是理解梅尼克所谓思想革命的起源与基础，那么我将把“历史主义”定义为最好地服务于达成这个目的的东西。定义的目标就在于抓住能够最好地解释梅尼克所谓革命的那个语词的意义。我将通过归纳那些对历史主义贡献最多的思想家的一般特征，来完成对历史主义的定义。
48	
49	Ernst Troeltsch, Der Historismus und seine Probleme, in Gesammelte Schriften (Tübingen: Mohr, 1922), III, 102.
50	
51	我们根据这样的指导，能够以类似恩斯特 · 特洛尔奇的方式很好地定义“历史主义”，特洛尔奇正是首位赋予这个词以现代含义的思想家。他认为，当“历史主义”被剥离一切偶然、否定的含义时，就意味着“我们有关人类及其文化与价值的所有思考的根本上的历史化”。  那么，我们思考的历史化究竟意味着什么呢？既然特洛尔奇没有提供进一步的说明，我们就必须代他而为之。大体上讲，历史化我们的思考就是说要认识到人类世界的一切东西—文化、价值、制度、实践、理性—都是由历史所造就的，因此没有任何东西具有永恒的形式、固定的本质以及超越历史变化的恒常认同。于是，历史主义者坚持一切人类世界事物的本质、认同与性质都是由历史形成的，它完全是将其变成存在的特殊历史进程的产物。换句话说，人类事物之中不存在永恒的实质与变化的偶然之间的区分，因为它们的实质本身就是历史的产物。为人类事物带来存在的特别原因同时也是它们是如此这般事物的原因；而这些原因彻底是历史的，也就是说它们依赖于特殊的语境和确定的时空。因而历史主义者就是有关人类世界的赫拉克利特主义者： 一切事物都处在流变之中；没有人能两次踏入历史的河流。
52	
53	这样的论题看上去非常形而上，甚至几乎触及宗教。很少有人会对历史主义经常被描述为一种世界观而感到奇怪。但真正给予历史主义全部力量与合理性的正是它在现代科学中的根源。历史主义脱胎于开创人类世界科学的尝试，这一科学与自然科学并驾齐驱。历史主义的普遍论点紧随两个完美的合理假定而来，这两个假定都是其科学程序不可缺少的东西。第一个假定是所有存在或发生于人类世界的事物都有一个充足的理由。第二个假定是这些理由都具有历史性，意即它们取决于特殊的时间背景、特定时间的特殊环境。这两个假定共同意味着人类世界的事物是其历史原因的产物，由其特殊的时间背景所造就。
54	
55	从一个非常普遍的角度来看，历史主义正是自然主义的对立面。自然主义声称自然世界的事物原则上可以通过科学得到说明，历史主义声称历史世界的事物原则上也可以通过科学加以澄清。自然主义最终导致的自然史拒斥稳定的种属与永恒的分类，历史主义同样拒绝永恒人性或理性。历史主义只是吸取自然史的教训，把它应用到人类世界之上。
56	
57	虽然历史主义可以与自然主义类比，但它并不就是后者的一个分支或形式，即不是将自然科学的规律与方法直接套用于人类世界。历史主义者未必同意人类世界的事物能够通过自然世界有效的相同方法与规律得到解释。历史主义者可以做出这样的说明，但他并不需要这么做。历史与自然科学方法的真正关系问题正是历史主义内部一个令人焦虑的事项。部分历史主义者认为这些方法间存在根本的差异，然而另外一些人则坚持它们本质上是一样的。这两派都是历史主义者，他们均赞同历史主义的一般论点，即人类世界的事物随历史而变化。他们也都觉得历史能够成为一门宽泛意义上的科学，亦即一套严格遵循认识论标准的获取知识的方法体系；他们仅仅对于历史研究的具体方法持有不同的观念。
58	
59	参见Meinecke, Historismus, pp.1—10, and Troeltsch, Der Historismus und seine Probleme, pp.103—106, 372—375, 381。我在自己之前的文章中采纳了这样的区分，参见“Historicism” , The Oxford Handbook of Continental Philosophy, eds. Brian Leiter and Michael Rosen (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2007), pp.155—179。而基于文中陈述的理由，我现在拒斥这样的区分。梅尼克与特洛尔奇认为自然科学的解释模式只与实证主义相关，而实证主义直到19世纪40年代才成为一种有影响力的思想力量。例如，参见Troeltsch, Der Historismus und seine Probleme, pp.371—375。他们从而低估了赫尔德、默泽尔以及洪堡的“人的科学”计划的重要性。这种苏格兰启蒙运动的计划对德国思想家们的影响成为最近许多历史研究的主题。参见下文，第三章第2节以及第四章第6节。
60	
61	历史主义经常被拿来与自然主义进行对比，好像对它的认同就在于主张历史知识方法是独特的，在类型上与自然科学的方法划清了界限。这正是梅尼克、特洛尔奇以及许多其他思想家的立场。  然而，这一观点伴随着两大突出的问题。首先，事实上只有很少的历史主义者坚持历史的方法与自然科学的方法在本质上有所不同。这一普遍化观点在19世纪末德罗伊森与狄尔泰身上体现得尤为明显，他们坚信理解（Verstehen）这一方法明确地与自然主义相对。但是，如此单以方法论术语定义历史主义的方式严重限制了这些术语的外延。这使得历史主义传统分成两大部分—如果它们根本上能够合为一体的话。其次，历史主义生发自18世纪自然主义的程序，力求将牛顿物理学的方法和法则运用到历史之上，从而创建一门“关于人的科学  ”。那些历史主义传统的奠基者—克拉德尼乌斯、默泽尔、赫尔德和洪堡—实际上都是这种自然主义程序的捍卫者。历史主义的研究者—尤其是梅尼克—认同并且强调这些思想家的奠定性角色。因此如果我们要在历史主义与自然主义间进行严格区分的话，那么上述这些人都将被逐出历史主义传统之外，而极少数学者能够接受这种主张。既然历史主义传统与自然主义相对立是晚近的发展，仅仅在19世纪晚期由德罗伊森和狄尔泰发起，那么任何反自然主义的历史主义观念都是时代的误置。
62	
63	参见Meinecke,Entstehung des Historismus, pp.155, 369, 595; and Troeltsch,Der Historismus und seine Probleme, pp.277—313。两人都强调了这些原则的活力论形而上学起源，无论它们是来自莱布尼茨（梅尼克的观点）还是谢林（特洛尔奇的观点）。这种形而上学确实在历史主义的早期阶段起到了重要的作用，而它在后来的阶段渐渐失去了核心地位；实际上存在着针对它的反动。整体论在狄尔泰、齐美尔与韦伯的著作中仍然显著，但它更多是方法论的而非形而上学的。
64	
65	除了“无所不在地关注历史变化”这一中心议题之外，还有另外两条可供界定的原则。  第一条是个体性原则。这条原则在历史主义传统中拥有许多含义，它的精确内涵取决于自身语境。它在最宽泛的意义上指的是： 历史界定的主体事项和历史探询的目标是个体，即实存于特定时间与空间之内的限定性个人、行动、文化或者时代。这条原则可追溯至柏拉图与亚里士多德，不过历史主义赋予了它新的意义。历史主义与那些古典时代的先驱不同，前者认为事物的个体性使得一个事物不同于其他事物，它与无视个体间差别、关注普遍化和法则的事物普遍性一样都是科学的对象。第二条原则是整体论，它的粗略含义就是整体优先于并且无法被还原成各个组成部分。从赫尔德至韦伯，整体论一直是历史主义的核心标志性特征。历史主义者坚称个人不是自足的、独立的单元，其认同和实存取决于这一部分所属的全部更广阔的社会、历史与文化世界中的位置。根据整体论的观点，社会、国家、文化抑或时代不是一种叠加和复合，而是每一部分能够独立于整体而实存；而这一整体本身无法被分割，并且决定其所辖的各个部分，这些部分无法离开整体而单独存在。主张整体能被还原为其部分的原子论被当作陈旧的机械论思维模式而遭到摒弃。很明显，这些原则紧密地相互联系，个体被理解成无法简化的整体或全体，反之亦然。
66	
67	经典的研究来自Pierre Duhem, Le système du monde: histoire des doctrines cosmologiques de Platon à Copernic (Paris: Hermann, 1954—1973)。关于这个议题的讨论，参见Frederick Copleston, A History of Philosophy: Late Medieval and Renaissance Philosophy (New York: Doubleday, 1963), III, 165—169；and E.J. Dijksterhuis, The Mechanization of the World Picture (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1961), pp.164—170。
68	
69	历史主义的核心主题在这些原则背后隐含着一个古老的哲学传统—唯名论，它可以追溯到14世纪的奥卡姆的威廉。唯名论对于早期近代科学主要代表人物（培根、霍布斯、洛克、格兰维尔、休谟）的重要性已是定论。  同样，唯名论对那些历史主义者（尤其是克拉德尼乌斯、赫尔德、兰克、李凯尔特、齐美尔以及韦伯）的思想起到了重要影响，这些人以不同的方式明确了这点。唯名论者认为任何实存的东西都是确定的或特殊的，而共相只是我们心理活动的产物，既不在事物之内，也不在单独的可知世界之中。这一命题是历史主义若干核心学说的理论依据。首先，它解释了历史主义对无所不在的变化的强调，因为他们把永恒的本质与固定的形式从历史的流动中排除了出去。历史主义者和真正的唯名论者相同，把这些本质与形式视作原质和抽象对象的物化。其次，唯名论也充当了历史主义个体性原则的根据与来源。历史主义之所以把个体设定为历史的目标与主体对象，就在于它认定只有个体才是真实的。在唯名论立场看来，历史主义者可以宣称历史是最为真实的科学。毕竟只有它聚焦于唯一真实的特殊性，而其他科学比如物理和化学努力形成普遍的规律，把具体的实在抛在一边。最后，唯名论还是常与历史主义相伴的相对主义的来源。唯名论的观念使得历史主义要求历史学家敬重一项特殊的方法论规范，即精确，从而去确定行动的原因以及特定思想与意图中的表现。思想、意图、价值抑或信仰的含义和目的离不开确定的语境、行动以及表达它们的言语。既然这些表达和具象各不相同、无法通约，因此人类本质、理性或者价值也就没有单一的形式。无视理性、价值和人类本质的特殊表达与具象普遍地谈论它们就是对纯粹抽象的沉迷。
70	
71	Aristotle, Metaphysics, Book V, 11, 1018b, 30—36; Book IX, 8, 1050a, 3—20.没有人比卡尔 · 波普尔带来了更多的混淆，他把本质主义视为历史主义的特征。特别参见The Poverty of Historicism, pp.26—34。同时参见The Open Society and Its Enemies (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1950), pp.34—36, 206—218。波普尔将本质主义赋予齐美尔与韦伯，说明他没有好好研究他们。
72	
73	尽管历史主义的唯名论特征显得异常显著并具有根本性，但它常常被人们忽略。确实，流行观点认为，历史主义出于其整体论的因素而与形而上学脱不开干系。整体论看上去对抽象实体和共相做出承诺，这些东西都独立于并且优先于组成它们的部分而存在，这和唯名论的观点针锋相对。唯名论看似应该拒斥整体论，因为它坚持个别自身具有自足性和独立存在，整体就应当是一种抽象和个别的复合。然而，我们应当重视的是： 整体论与唯名论可以完美地兼容。整体论无须对共相的存在做出任何承诺： 整体同样可被看作个体，而它的组成部分变成它的抽象产物。整体论者无须主张整体独立于其部分而实存；他能坚称整体只有在部分中或者通过部分而存在，这样整体只具有相对于组成部分的逻辑上和解释上的优先性。正如亚里士多德在很久以前教导的那样，存在层面处于第一位的东西（殊相），与解释或推理层面处于第一位的东西（共相）之间并不需要同一。  看上去吊诡的唯名论的整体论或者整体论的唯名论充当了历史主义传统基本的、共同的特征。将历史主义与本质论、存在论、神秘论乃至任何有关抽象实体的信仰联系在一起乃是深刻的误解，甚至是一种歪曲。
74	
75	### 2. 历史学作为一门科学
76	
77	赋予这些人物共同的目标或议程并不意味着他们形成了有意识的运动或传统。有必要强调的是，作为代表特定思想传统的历史主义概念严格来说是历史学家时代误置的建构。许多属于这一传统的思想家并不会自称“历史主义者”；实际上在（转下页）（接上页）19世纪末，当“历史主义”一词出现并得到广泛应用，同时获得贬义内涵的时候，有些人坚决拒斥了这个标签。这种情况发生在狄尔泰、齐美尔、文德尔班、李凯尔特以及拉斯克的身上，他们将“历史主义”等同于“相对主义”。Johannes Hof fmeister, “Wissenschaft” , in Wörterbuch der philosophischen Begrif fe (Hamburg: Meiner, 1955), pp.673—674.
78	
79	历史主义不只是一种抽象的思维倾向，而是历史化人类世界思维的尝试。它的议题、目标和模式使其成为单一的、连贯的、持续的思想传统。  该议题简单而充满雄心： 把历史学合法化为一门科学。这一目标并不意味着使历史学成为科学—因为虽然有争议，但历史自从文艺复兴以来就已成为科学—而是论证什么东西让历史学成为科学。所有归属于历史主义传统的思想家，无论他们是自然主义者还是反自然主义者，都希望证明历史学的科学性质。他们在宽泛的意义上使用“科学”一词，对应德语中的“科学”（Wissenschaft），即某些能够获得知识的方法途径。  尽管历史主义者有关这种“科学”的观念各不相同甚至相互冲突，但不妨碍他们共享着证明历史的科学性的相同目标。历史主义的思想革命与这种对待历史的全新态度相互配合，形成了历史学可以凭借自身成为一门科学的现代信念，它应该具备所有新自然科学的性质与特权。

181	怀疑论者即使同意上述这些观点，也会否认将科学地位赋予历史。因为即使我们承认历史造就了我们的样子，但这对确定过去到底发生了什么毫无裨益。毕竟我们无法仅通过内省来了解过去。我们无法逃避的是，关于过去的认知是一项艰苦的侦探工作，须通过我们在记录和遗迹中发现的只鳞片甲的信息、证据来进行理解和重构。但是这种重构看上去与科学所要求的确定性相去甚远。历史主义者在此再次做好了应对怀疑论的准备。克拉德尼乌斯在18世纪50年代率先回应这一挑战，而他有关推理态度的许多方面代表了整体传统。1751年，克拉德尼乌斯在《历史学通论》中反驳了历史的皮浪主义者，前者宣称历史探询具有关于知识的特有标准，而且它应该由这样的标准自己来评判，不去求助无法达到的论证准则。既然历史知识经常具有不确定性，那么人们出于其不可论证的原因而大范围地加以质疑便是毫无意义的行为。就像亚里士多德所说的那样，我们不能在学科题材所允许的程度之外期待更强的严密性。  当然，我们可以质疑许多历史命题，但那只是由于命题与适用历史的证据标准不相符，而不是因为无法以几何学方式证明它。克拉德尼乌斯尽可能详尽地说明了历史学家在搜集和评估证据时应当遵循的特定规则。这些规则保障了标准和严密性，只要历史学家遵从它们，它们就能提供有关主题的充分确定性，或者至少是没能获得过的确定性，而这样的确定性同样是科学的特征。

183	### 5. 社会与历史语境
184	
185	历史主义的根本性原则在于： 一切人类行动与观念必须从它们的特殊历史因果性与语境出发得到历史性的解释。该原则是自反的，当然也能适用于历史主义自身。它同样只有在被置于其特殊的社会与历史语境中才是可以理解的。

Worldbreaking

WHERE WE WENT WRONG

One must always know the boundaries with great precision.

—FRIEDRICH AUGUST WOLF, ENCYCLOPÄDIE DER PHILOLOGIE1

WE  DO  NOT  NORMALLY  STUDY  or  teach  ancient  history  in  this  manner.  Why
not?  Had  certain  trends  continued,  we  might  have  embraced  a  globalizing
vision a long time ago. But as it happened, scholarship took a very different
turn, leading us farther and farther away from inclusive, humanity-centered
approaches.  The  world  the  worldbuilders  made  was  broken  up,  smashed
into pieces by their learned descendants.

The  story  of  how  this  unfolded  would  fill  a  much  longer  book.  It
certainly  deserves  one.  All  I  can  do  here  is  engage  with  traditions  of
scholarship  that  have  become  dominant  in  Western  countries.  I  focus  in
particular  on  developments  in  intellectual  and  academic  circles  in
eighteenth-  and  nineteenth-century  Germany,  which  proved
to  be
disproportionately influential. Just as contemporary universities around the
globe are profoundly indebted to the German model of organizing research
and  teaching,  so  are  the  ways  in  which  we  have  learned  to  deal  with  the
remains of the ancient world.

possible, did not foster a global perspective of the human past. I show how

This is, however, easier said than done. I am not aware of any academic
system  that  fully  incorporates  the  entire  ancient  world  into  History
programs.  To  name  just  one  example,  in  Germany,  where  the  holistic
Classics template has been almost completely abandoned, only historians of
ancient  Greece  and  Rome  are  routinely  admitted  to  History  departments.
Worse still, in institutions that employ a sufficiently large number of these
scholars  they  tend  to  form  their  own  subunits  within  larger  History
programs. This encourages even greater fragmentation than that fostered by
Classics,  as Greco-Roman  historians  end up being  institutionally detached
from those who study other aspects of Greece and Rome, or other parts of
the ancient world, or more recent history—an outcome that is in a sense the

 worst  of  all  possible  worlds.  Much  German  scholarship  in  this  area  bears
the scars of this multiple isolation.82

And  while  other  national  traditions  may  differ  in  specific  ways,  these
problems  tend  to  be  widespread.  The  disappearance  of  the  model  of
Altertumswissenschaft  from  continental  Europe  has  generally  failed  to
promote  more  inclusive  ancient  studies.  Thus,  while  the  dismantling  of
Classics  is  a  necessary  precondition  for  establishing  a  viable  field  of
planetary foundational history, it is clearly not sufficient.

German academia also highlights the challenges of teamwork as a means
of  globalizing  early  history.  There,  governmental  entities  and  foundations
have  long  been  providing  relatively  generous  funding  for  collaborative
projects  and  initiatives  in  the  humanities,  including  historical  fields.  Yet
none  of  this  has  led  to  any  discernible  reorientation  of  scholarly  practice.
The reason for this is not hard to find: such arrangements clash with deeply
entrenched  modes  of  training,  hiring,  evaluation,  and  promotion  that  are
predicated  on  and  promote  academic  individualism  across  the  humanities.

structures.  In  this  context,  teamwork  tends  to  remain  opportunistic  and
short-term, deployed as a means of bridging funding and employment gaps
between individualized training and individualized teaching and research.

This  raises  an  obvious  question:  what,  in  light  of  all  of  this,  can  we
actually  hope  to  accomplish?  It  is  all  well  and  good  to  criticize  current
practices, and to imagine how things might or should be done instead. But
we must also confront the thorny issue of feasibility.

There is no shortage of different ways to globalize ancient history. So, what
are the obstacles? Reduced to essentials, the urge to compartmentalize the

niche specialization. But we ought to be wary of conflating two issues: the
desire for mastery, and the need. They are not the same.

# What Is Ancient History? — Chapters 2-4

## Worldbreaking

WHERE WE WENT WRONG

One must always know the boundaries with great precision.

—FRIEDRICH AUGUST WOLF, ENCYCLOPÄDIE DER PHILOLOGIE1

WE DO NOT NORMALLY STUDY or teach ancient history in this manner. Why not? Had certain trends continued, we might have embraced a globalizing vision a long time ago. But as it happened, scholarship took a very different turn, leading us farther and farther away from inclusive, humanity-centered approaches. The world the worldbuilders made was broken up, smashed into pieces by their learned descendants.

The story of how this unfolded would fill a much longer book. It certainly deserves one. All I can do here is engage with traditions of scholarship that have become dominant in Western countries. I focus in particular on developments in intellectual and academic circles in eighteenth- and nineteenth-century Germany, which proved to be disproportionately influential. Just as contemporary universities around the globe are profoundly indebted to the German model of organizing research and teaching, so are the ways in which we have learned to deal with the remains of the ancient world.

In this chapter, I ask why the unprecedented expansion of connectivity on a planetary scale of the last few hundred years, and the equally unprecedented expansion and exchange of historical knowledge it made possible, did not foster a global perspective of the human past. I show how professionalization, nationalism, and racism interacted to create an academic landscape carved up into ever-smaller parcels that became separated by increasingly impermeable boundaries; and how a novel form of worship of ancient Greece and Rome provided a model of conceptual segregation that boosted these divisions while securing an exceptionally privileged position for those two cultures—so privileged in fact that they came to be equated with “ancient history” as such while broader perspectives fell by the wayside. I move back and forth between different levels of resolution—the study of Greece and Rome, of antiquity, and of history in general—all of which contributed to setting the course for our engagement with the ancient past.

Even though my survey is necessarily highly selective (or even reductive, not to mention disrespectful), my main point should not be controversial: that over the last 250 years, academic ideals and practices have made it ever harder for us to explore, understand, and publicize our shared foundational history. In an apparent paradox, these trends gained momentum just as spectacular advances in the decipherment of ancient scripts and languages together with the rise of archaeological fieldwork made such a foundational history feasible for the first time.

Matching our knowledge of that history with a vision that does it justice remains a task for us today and for future generations. In this respect, the history of scholarship has an important role to play: by reminding us how much scholarship has changed in the past, it gives us hope that it can do so again. If we want to understand where we are, we must know how we got here. That understanding is not merely an end in itself: it is both a necessary step toward reform—to re-forming our habits of engagement and inquiry—and a safeguard against repeating the mistakes of the past.

### Bigger Histories for a Bigger World

I began the introduction to this book by pointing out how, in Western countries, the term “ancient history” tends to have a narrow meaning, commonly limited to the history of Greece and Rome with or without their immediate neighbors. One might think that this is not a big deal, even natural—why wouldn’t societies privilege the early history of their own corner of the globe and their cultural forebears, real or imagined? And of course historiography has always been mostly local, regional, or ethnic in focus. At the same time, however, ecumenically minded historians had long tried to keep track of widening horizons. As connections between different parts of the world expanded, so did historical vision.2

=== tail ===

To some extent this imbalance may be attributed to the very existence of Classics and other ancient area studies fields. At (usually better-resourced) institutions that maintain such programs, it is perfectly rational for History departments to minimize or eliminate investment in the ancient world and reserve precious faculty positions for other specialisms. The abolition of separate ancient area studies programs would make this attitude harder to justify.

Even so, Classics and cognate programs bear only part of the blame. The demotion of the more distant past also stems from a more general tendency, that of focusing research and (perhaps especially) teaching on more recent periods of history that can be more readily and more directly connected to current conditions. Such presentist undercurrents can never be fully eliminated, nor should they be. It is perfectly reasonable to turn to whatever history promises to throw the most light on the roads that were taken (or not taken) in making our world, and on what was lost in the process. Ancient historians must mobilize this curiosity for their own purposes by making the strongest possible case for the profound relevance of their subject matter for understanding the present. This, of course, is the whole point of reframing “ancient” history as “foundational” history.

This is, however, easier said than done. I am not aware of any academic system that fully incorporates the entire ancient world into History programs. To name just one example, in Germany, where the holistic Classics template has been almost completely abandoned, only historians of ancient Greece and Rome are routinely admitted to History departments. Worse still, in institutions that employ a sufficiently large number of these scholars they tend to form their own subunits within larger History programs. This encourages even greater fragmentation than that fostered by Classics, as Greco-Roman historians end up being institutionally detached from those who study other aspects of Greece and Rome, or other parts of the ancient world, or more recent history—an outcome that is in a sense the worst of all possible worlds. Much German scholarship in this area bears the scars of this multiple isolation.82

And while other national traditions may differ in specific ways, these problems tend to be widespread. The disappearance of the model of Altertumswissenschaft from continental Europe has generally failed to promote more inclusive ancient studies. Thus, while the dismantling of Classics is a necessary precondition for establishing a viable field of planetary foundational history, it is clearly not sufficient.

German academia also highlights the challenges of teamwork as a means of globalizing early history. There, governmental entities and foundations have long been providing relatively generous funding for collaborative projects and initiatives in the humanities, including historical fields. Yet none of this has led to any discernible reorientation of scholarly practice. The reason for this is not hard to find: such arrangements clash with deeply entrenched modes of training, hiring, evaluation, and promotion that are predicated on and promote academic individualism across the humanities. Efforts to support collaboration do not align with underlying incentive structures. In this context, teamwork tends to remain opportunistic and short-term, deployed as a means of bridging funding and employment gaps between individualized training and individualized teaching and research.

This raises an obvious question: what, in light of all of this, can we actually hope to accomplish? It is all well and good to criticize current practices, and to imagine how things might or should be done instead. But we must also confront the thorny issue of feasibility.

It is possible to get an idea of the whole from a portion, but impossible to acquire knowledge and accurate understanding.

### Putting Ancient History Back Together Again

In the first chapter, I argued that those of our ancestors whom we to like call “ancient” laid the foundations for the world we inhabit now. They did so for better or worse—creating novel opportunities, choking off older lifeways, and nudging their descendants away from alternative paths of development in a heady mix of variability and convergence, of contingencies and persistent trends, of roads not taken and the growing dominance of a particular bundle of norms, practices, expectations, and realities. In the end, this process was global in nature: although it did not unfold everywhere or at the same time, it slowly but surely swallowed up our entire species.

A process that was global in both scope and impact ought to be studied and taught in ways that are true to that scope and impact. This certainly does not mean that history always ought to be approached on a planetary scale: that is just one option among many, and often not the most useful one or even unfeasible. What it does mean, however, is that we must seek to take proper account of broader connections, patterns, and dynamics no matter how small and local the cases we study happen to be. We can do this in ways that suit a wide variety of needs and preferences. As we saw in the previous chapter, historians have for many generations moved further and further away from that premise. Shattering the one world they were charged with understanding, they carved up its history into more and more fragments, conjuring up smaller and smaller worlds, truncating and trapping the human experience in ever-tighter cages. Worse still, for a long time Western academics focused on gilding one particular cage (which housed the Greeks and Romans) at the expense of others. After a quarter of a millennium of these efforts, the manner we view, study, and teach our shared foundations has come to be seriously out of whack.

As we saw in the second chapter, these processes unfolded in the context of much broader intellectual trends and power dynamics. At the same time, the study of GreeceandRome the precocious embodied and modeled all these divisive principles with prophetic clarity and persuasive authority. Where this format still lives on, primarily in North America, the British Isles, and Australasia, it prevents any future

institutionalization of consolidation of our engagement with the ancient world. There are three reasons for this.

First, its label and residual privilege among area studies fields in the Anglo-American university scene marks out Classics as somehow special and therefore worthy of special attention and commitments. That all by itself arrests the development of globalized scholarship and teaching on the ancient world. More specifically, this relative privileging of Classics prioritizes Greek and Roman history in ways that curtail engagement with other and generally (even) less funded ancient histories.

Second, in a considerable number of academic institutions, Classics partly or entirely absorbs the study and teaching of the history of the Greco-Roman world, an area that thanks to its rich documentation and exceptionally deep scholarly penetration will always be an essential element of any global foundational history. By laying claim to this essential element, Classics isolates and detaches it from the study of other ancient histories as well as from intellectual currents in the History profession at large. Both of these barriers interfere with globalizing perspectives.

Third, embedding professional historians of Greece and Rome in the Classics template not only separates them from other ancient historians and from historians more generally but in practice tends to ensnare them in the “language trap” that I discussed in the previous chapter.

None of these dynamics are conducive to the globalization of ancient history that I sketched out in chapters 1 and 3. In all these respects, for ancient historians the Classics model and its corollaries ought to serve as a model of how not to go about our business.

To be sure, globalizing ancient history is not the measure of all things. Perhaps Classics as an organizing principle is imbued with so many other virtues that they outweigh these concerns. But that is not the case. The field of Classics in and of itself is deeply flawed and obsolete.

# Preface — Disciplining Classics / Altertumswissenschaft als Beruf

The articles collected in the present volume explore a few aspects of the role which has been played within the recent history of various kinds of Classical scholarship by three processes of considerable general importance in the sociology of knowledge: disciplinization, institutionalization, and professionalization. To be sure, for certain features of these three processes there were ample pre-modern and early modern partial precedents and parallels, in Europe and elsewhere; but it has been the establishment, the stabilization, and above all the systematic interrelation of all three of them which have so deeply transformed the study of classical antiquity and of other fields over the past several centuries in Europe and America, and more recently in the other parts of the world which have been more or less profoundly influenced by the Western model. Though all three processes are closely related, particularly as they have been put into effect in the past two centuries, nonetheless each term picks out a somewhat different set of features within a complex set of developments and they can be distinguished conceptually.

Disciplinization denotes the establishment of a defined field of objects of knowledge and of a set of methods designed to study it in a regulated and inter-subjectively verifiable manner, in such a way as both to create a stable body of information which can be exchanged, examined, and modified synchronically among contemporary researchers on that field and to insure its diachronic transmission to future generations of researchers. Kant’s distinction between a “Wissenschaft” as a systematically interrelated body of knowledge on the one hand and any mere aggregate of unrelated information on the other played a key role in the imposition of disciplinarity upon certain earlier methods of study at the turn of the 19th century and remains enormously, if subliminally, influential. Disciplinization is above all methodological in nature and involves a set of related sub-processes, such as abstraction, formalization, specification, and generalization.

Institutionalization refers to the creation of trans-personal organizational systems for the furtherance of specified goals (such as the study of these disciplines) which are taken to be of sufficient importance for society as a whole to justify a substantial financial subvention which will benefit not only in the short term the specific individuals who participate in them but also in the long term an uncertain but presumably larger number of unknown future participants and unknown possible recipients of prospective advantages. Institutionalization secures an at least minimally long-term duration of focused and hence hopefully productive collaboration by distinguishing between functions on the one hand and the individuals who come to fulfill them more or less well and thereby to transform them on the other hand. This is above all an administrative phenomenon and coordinates such sub-processes as legislation, recruitment, career definition, and segmentation.

Professionalization, finally, designates the set of transformative processes which individuals are made to undergo so as to make them appear suitable for fulfilling the functions out of which these institutions are composed. Some tribes have rites of passage, others have Promotionen and Habilitationen, dissertations or théses. Before bestowing upon certain already mature adults the reward of a life-long sinecure, society takes a final opportunity to humiliate them by obliging them to fulfil requirements which, however sophisticated their scientific justification, also serve to remind the candidates, who are on the point of joining the bosses, that, however high the value that they themselves may have assigned to their merits, these alone would never have guaranteed them success: the final kick in the pants not only provides an additional impetus for the movement upwards but will also leave psychic bruises which the new boss will alleviate by distributing kicks of his own upon those who are at first only slightly younger than he is. This is above all an anthropological and psychological phenomenon and links with one another procedures of regulation, evaluation, and adjudication, definitions of competence and pertinence, and distinctions between sometimes finely shaded degrees of public and private.

The transformation in Classical studies between the end of the 18th and the beginning of the 19th century was one of the most spectacular, successful, and influential of the many processes of scientific modernization which have been determined by these three processes over the past several centuries. The story of the gradual propagation of modern methods and institutions of Classical philology from the seminars of Göttingen in the mid-18th century, through the courses of Friedrich August Wolf at the end of that century, to the establishment of the University of Berlin and the Humanistic Gymnasium in Prussia at the beginning of the next century, and from there (as well as from other sources, including Bavaria) to the rest of Germany, and, with some resistance, to Europe and the world, is a remarkable one. This story usually used to be told (and sometimes still is) in progressivist, unquestioningly positive, indeed occasionally almost hagiographic terms.! Now matters are changing. The crisis in which the field of Classics has found itself for a long time (in some senses, since the beginning) has led to wide-spread confusion, consternation, and complaint, but also, in at least a few cases, to a more sober analysis of the forces which supported and resisted and the mechanisms that rendered possible the transformation to a development which was, precisely, not inevitable and not even very likely. Recent studies of the disciplinization, institutionalization, and professionalization of modern scientific methods in Germany,” England,3 and France‘ have either focused upon the paradigm of Classical philology as a particularly rich and exemplary case or at the very least have important implications for the future study of the history of that field. Wedding the sociology of knowledge to the history of philological method, Pierre Bourdieu to Rudolf Pfeiffer, may tax the imaginative resources of even the most committed interdisciplinarist; but as the fruit from such a union might well issue forth new and more convincing ways of conceiving the history of Classical studies within their social, educational, and scientific contexts.

Instead of emphasizing the central steps of the transformation of modern Classical studies in Germany at the turn of the 19th century, which have been studied often (though not definitively), the essays gathered in this volume illuminate certain less familiar aspects of these general trends. A first group of three essays considers some particularly interesting examples of tendencies in pre-modern Classical studies which pointed in certain ways towards later changes but which at the same time indicate the resistances against which the institutionalization of the field had, has had, and has to struggle. A second group of five essays examines the crisis in German Altertumswissenschaft during the last third of the 19th century signalled by the criticisms of Friedrich Nietzsche, and broadens the scope of inquiry to include other developments at the turn of the 20th century. A final group of three essays analyses the question of the disciplinarity of Classics as it is posed in the immediate present and makes suggestions concerning future prospects and challenges. Thus the temporal span of this volume reaches from the 17th century in France to our own days and the foreseeable future. In terms of scholarly disciplines, the emphasis in this, as in the preceding volumes of this series, is upon the university practice of Classical philology; but additional light is thrown upon this field by consideration of related issues in European and American school education, papyrology, and cultural studies, and in the role of philology in the modernization of China. It is particularly worth noting that in this volume, devoted to the professionalization of Classical studies, more than half of the essays have been written by young scholars who stand at the beginning of their own professional careers.

This volume is derived from a conference on the subject of the professionalization and institutionalization of philology which was held in conjunction with the Internationales Wissenschaftsforum at Heidelberg University from 2-4 July 1999. As in the previous conferences in this series, which led to the publication of the volumes Collecting Fragments — Fragmente sammeln. Aporemata 1 in 1997, Editing Texts — Texte edieren. Aporemata 2 in 1998, Commentaries — Kommentare. Aporemata 4 in 1999, and Historicization — Historisierung. Aporemata 5 in 2001, the purpose was to explore historical and theoretical aspects of a scholarly practice which has played, and continues to play, an important role in the study of ancient Greece and Rome, as well as of many other cultures. This is the final volume in that series.

Although this volume is derived from a conference, it does not simply reproduce the papers presented there: all have been modified, some have been added, others have been omitted. It is hoped that the resulting volume will display even more coherence and unity than the colloquium did, while retaining something of its liveliness and diversity. Besides the authors whose articles are published here, the following scholars also participated in the discussions: Daniel Boyarin (Berkeley), Lorraine Daston (Berlin), Carlotta Dionisotti (London), Luca Giuliani (Munich), Anthony Grafton (Princeton), Andreas Kablitz (Cologne), Stefan Maul (Heidelberg). Funding for this conference, as for all of its predecessors, was provided by a Leibniz prize of the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft; in the present case, additional support was provided by the Fritz Thyssen Stiftung (Cologne) and by the Stiftung Universitét Heidelberg. The staff of the Internationales Wissenschaftsforum, especially Dr. Theresa Reiter and Gudrun Strehlow, were uniformly friendly, helpful, and unruffled. The administrative organization of the conference was carried out with typical patience and inventiveness by Dr. Helga Kohler. The editorial work on this volume, including the preparation of the indices (but not their lemmatization, for which I must take the blame), was performed with grace, skill, and infinite good humor by Ingeborg von Appen; she was assisted in many ways by Dr. Manuel Baumbach and Dagmar Schweinfurth.

At the conclusion of this lengthy, intense, and (at least for me personally) highly satisfying project, I would like now once again, and for a last time, to express my heartfelt gratitude to the many students, friends, colleagues, and associates who have been involved in it for their generous and helpful contributions.

178	 -or sources-for being reliable, but we praise non-contemporary histori ans
179	 -or derivative authorities-for displaying sound judgment in the interpre-
180	 tation and evaluation of the original sources. This distinction between
181	 original authorities and non-contemporary historians became the comm on
182	 patrimony of historical research only in the late seventeenth century. The
183	 distinction is of course to be found before that time, but it was not formulated
184	 with any degree of accuracy or generally considered to be a necessary pre-
185	 supposition of historical study. In the formation of the new historical meth od
186	 -and consequently in the creation of modern historical writing on the ancient
187	 world-the so-called antiquaries played a conspicuous part and posed essential
188	 problems. They showed how to use non-literary evidence, but they also made
189	 people reflect on the difference between collecting facts and interpreting facts.
190	 It is the purpose of this essay to explain, first, the origins of antiquarian
191	 research; secondly, why the antiquaries played such a part in the reform of
192	 historical method in the eighteenth century; and finally, why in the nineteenth
193	 century it became increasingly evident that there was no longer any justifi-
194	 cation for making a distinction between antiquarian and historical studies.

1149	 In the seventeenth century religious and political disputations had per-
1150	 vaded history and discredited the historian. Bias was easily scented every-
1151	 where, and the natural conclusion was to distrust the whole tribe of historians.
1152	 At the same time attempts were made to put historical knowledge on a safer
1153	 basis by analysing the sources thoroughly and drawing, if possible, on other
1154	 evidence than that provided by past historians. A sceptical attitude prevailed,
1155	 but this scepticism did not always imply complete pessimism as to the possi-
1156	 bility of sound historical knowledge.'
1157	
1158	 Critical minds emphasized how little was known. La Mothe Le Vayer
1159	 formulated what was to become known as historical Pyrrhonism in his essay
1160	 of 1668: Du peu de certitude qu'il y a dans l'histoire. R. Simon and Bentley
1161	 showed to what lengths thorough criticism could go both on sacred and
1162	 profane history. In 1682 Bayle began to show his hand in the Critique gindrale
1163	 de 1'histoire du calvinisme, where he declared: "il est bien mal aise de parvenir
1164	 jusqu'i l'dvidence"; and also: "en un mot, il n'y a point de Filouterie plus
1165	 grande que celle qui se peut exercer sur les monumens historiques." In the
1166	 next decades intellectual Europe was overpowered by the massive erudition
1167	 and searching criticism of the Dictionnaire historique et critique, a best seller,
1168	 notwithstanding its dimensions. Ernst Cassirer once took Bayle as the proto-
1169	 type of the modern irudit who has no other concern than the increase of
1170	 knowledge.2 To contemporaries he was Bayle the sceptic, "l'illustre Bayle
1171	 qui apprend si bien & douter," as Baron Holbach sympathetically noted.3

1178	 of pioneer work in the comparative study of religion, of which the most
1179	 important product is the Demonstratio evangelica of 1672.4 Secondly, a refuta-

1251	 Historical Pyrrhonism was hitting both at traditional historical teaching
1252	 and at traditional religious beliefs.' It was only natural that members of
1253	 religious congregations (Bollandists, Maurists) should make some of the best
1254	 contributions towards distinguishing between reasonable and unreasonable
1255	 doubts in history. But the quest for safe historical rules was not confined to
1256	 them. The discussion on Pyrrhonism raged in German Protestant universities
1257	 which were just then making their first conspicuous contribution to his torical
1258	 method. The controversy passed from the hands of historians and philos ophers
1259	 to those of lawyers, who, being traditionally concerned with the reliability of
1260	 witnesses, could bring a great deal of experience to bear on this subject. All
1261	 these people tried to determine the characteristics of what they could call
1262	 reliable evidence. Books of rhetorical rules on the art of historical writing
1263	 were of course still produced. The Jesuits wrote a few classic ones of this
1264	 type (P. Rapin, P. Le Moyne). But a new type of treatise on historical writing
1265	 developed which broke away from the rhetorical Ars Historica of the Renais-
1266	 sance and was practically confined to the method of interpreting and criticiz-
1267	 ing sources. Some text-books were chiefly concerned with textual criticism
1268	 (authenticity and emendations of texts) : the Ars Critica by J. Le Clerc (1697)
1269	 is the most important of them. Others, like H. Griffet, Traite des difrfrentes
1270	 sortes de preuves qui servent i"tablir la verite' de l'histoire (1769) were mainly con-
1271	 cerned with the historical value of original authorities.

1442	 The study of the Holy Scriptures was only an extreme case of analysis of
1443	 a tradition almost unsupported by independent evidence. The formulation
1444	 of internal criteria sufficient to establish the bona fides of the sources was the
1445	 only way to answer the sceptic in the absence of independent documentary
1446	 sources or of any considerable amount of epigraphic and archaeological
1447	 material.' The whole discussion on the miracles of Jesus between Charles
1448	 Blount (168o) and Charles Leslie (1698) and between Th. Woolston (1727)
1449	 and Bishop Sherlock (1729) turned on the reliability of the writers of the
1450	 Gospels as witnesses. To Blount who implied that there is no better evidence
1451	 for the miracles of Jesus than for the miracles of Apollonius of Tyana, Leslie
1452	 replied by what he called his "Short and Easy Method" of selecting good
1453	 witnesses. Whether the method was as short and easy as Leslie thought is
1454	 another matter. Even when, under the influence of J. D. Michaelis, more
1455	 attention was given to Hebrew antiquities, the discussion of the bona fides
1456	 of the sources remained the main method of assessing the truth of the Bible.
1457	 In Roman History, Perizonius' Animadversiones Historicae (1685) were a
1458	
1459	 sound attempt at methodical analysis of literary evidence without much appeal
1460	 to documentary evidence. When the wave of historical Pyrrhonism was
1461	 dangerously mounting he defended his position, that of moderate criticism,
1462	 in his Oratio defide historiarum contra Pyrrhonismum Historicum (1702). His main
1463	 argument was that in certain cases historians can be trusted because they
1464	 speak against the interest of the cause they are defending.
1465	
1466	 Complex philological criticism such as Perizonius was attempting did not
1467	
1468	 come into its own until the beginning of the nineteenth century when a more
1469	 subtle technique enabled scholars to discover the literary sources (if any) of
1470	 literary sources. In the eighteenth century nobody had yet any precise
1471	 notion of the sources of Diodorus or Tacitus. Nor as yet was the personality
1472	 of the historian himself an object of conspicuous interest, except in a few
1473	 cases. Also the idea that a tradition is entitled to respect as the mouthpiece
1474	 of popular beliefs did not command wide attention. As long as these aspects
1475	 were not carefully considered, it was inevitable that official documents,
1476	 inscriptions, and coins should appear more reliable than literary evidence
1477	 merely based on tradition. It was first of all a question of number. Common
1478	 sense would offer insuperable resistance to the notion that thousands of
1479	 documents, coins, and inscriptions could be forged as easily as isolated
1480	 literary texts.

import json, re, statistics

lay = json.load(open('_layout.json', encoding='utf-8'))

    'preserve and extend access to Journal of the Warburg',

    t = t.strip()
    if not t: return True
    if any(n in t for n in NOISE): return True
    if re.match(r'^ANCIENT HISTORY', t): return True
    if re.match(r'^[0-9IlOo]{2,4}\s+ARNALDO\s+MOMIGLIANO', t): return True
    if re.match(r'^\d{1,3}$', t): return True
    if re.match(r'^[IVXLOo0-9]{1,3}$', t): return True      # stray page numerals
    return False

HEADMAP = {}
for t, lv in [('Introduction',2),('I',2),('The Origins of Antiquarian Research',3),
              ('II',2),('of Historical Evidence',3),('(a) The Terms of the Controversy',4),
              ('(b) The Emphasis on Non-Literary Evidence',4),

              ('III',2),('(a) The Conflict in the z8th Century',4),
              ('(b) The Conflict in the Igth Century',4),
              ('APPENDIX I1',2),("John Leland, King's Antiquary",3),
              ('APPENDIX II2',2),('(about 1740-1840)',3)]:
    HEADMAP[t] = lv
MULTI_HEAD = {'The Controversy of the 17th and i8th Centuries on the Value': 3,
              'A Select List of Studies on Pre-Roman Italy': 3}

def narrow(l):
    return (l['x1'] <= 320) or (l['x0'] >= 230 and l['x1'] <= 630)

FN_START = re.compile(r'^\d{1,2}\s*[A-Z"\'(]')
SENT_END = '.!?"'
FIXES = [('p referred','preferred'),('infe rred','inferred'),('histori ans','historians'),
 ('comm on','common'),('meth od','method'),('systematicall y','systematically'),
 ('recognize d','recognized'),('Thoug h','Though'),('th e recent past','the recent past'),
 ('l ife','life'),('B ut','But'),('tex ts','texts'),('qua edam','quaedam'),
 ('whe reby','whereby'),('Monu ments','Monuments'),('can onical','canonical'),
 ('nesc io','nescio')]

blocks = []
for b in lay:
    if b['page'] == 0: continue
    lines = [l for l in b['lines'] if not is_noise(l['text']) and l['text'].strip()]
    if not lines: continue
    t0 = lines[0]['text'].strip()
    if t0 in HEADMAP and len(lines) == 1:
        blocks.append(('H', HEADMAP[t0], t0, b['page'])); continue
    if t0 in MULTI_HEAD:
        blocks.append(('H', MULTI_HEAD[t0], ' '.join(l['text'].strip() for l in lines), b['page'])); continue
    blocks.append(('B', 0, lines, b['page']))

page_blocks = {}
for blk in blocks:
    page_blocks.setdefault(blk[3], []).append(blk)
marked = []
for pg in sorted(page_blocks):
    bl = page_blocks[pg]; seen = False; fstart = None
    for idx, blk in enumerate(bl):
        if blk[0] != 'B': continue
        ls = blk[2]
        if not seen:
            if any(l['x0'] < 100 and l['x1'] > 380 for l in ls): seen = True
            continue
        if all(narrow(l) for l in ls):
            fstart = idx; break
    for idx, blk in enumerate(bl):
        marked.append((blk[0], blk[1], blk[2], fstart is not None and idx >= fstart))

def join(lines):
    s = ''
    for k, l in enumerate(lines):
        t = re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', l['text']).strip()
        s = t if k == 0 else (s + t if s.endswith('-') else s + ' ' + t)
    return s

def paras(lines, fn):
    out, cur = [], []
    n = len(lines)
    for i, l in enumerate(lines):
        cur.append(l)
        if i == n-1:
            out.append(cur); break
        nx = lines[i+1]
        win = [lines[j] for j in range(max(0,i-4), min(n,i+4))]
        wx = [q['x1'] for q in win]
        wl = [len(q['text'].strip()) for q in win]
        med = statistics.median(wl)
        dy = l['y0'] - nx['y0']; dx = nx['x0'] - l['x0']
        brk = (dy >= 15 and fn) or (dy >= 16 and not fn) \
              or (dx >= 9 and fn) or (dx >= 14 and not fn) \
              or bool(FN_START.match(nx['text'].strip())) \
              or (l['x1'] < 0.72*max(wx) and len(l['text'].strip()) < 0.72*med)
        if brk:
            out.append(cur); cur = []
    return [join(p) for p in out]

    blk = marked[i]
    if blk[0] == 'H':

    fn = blk[3]; grp = []; j = i
    while j < len(marked) and marked[j][0] == 'B' and marked[j][3] == fn:

    i = j

    buckets = {}
    for l in grp:

    cols = []
    for k in sorted(buckets):

    for ci, col in enumerate(cols):

            prev = merged.pop()
            sep = '' if prev.endswith('-') else ' '
            col = [prev + sep + col[0]] + col[1:]
        merged.extend(col)
    for p in merged: final.append(('P', 0, p))

text = ''
for t in final:
    if t[0] == 'H':

    text = text.replace(a, b)
with open('_out_body.txt', 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    f.write(text)
print('emitted', len(final))

Ancient history was still written as part of universal history (a tradition especially cherished by Protestant universities), but the section on Greece and Rome of a universal history would practically amount to a summary of the ancient sources in the right chronological order-hardly the business of serious students of "antiquitas."1

153	The antiquaries, by collecting much of their evidence outside the literary sources, helped to make the need for new histories apparent. 163	
164	In the seventeenth century religious and political disputations had per-vaded history and discredited the historian. Bias was easily scented every-where, and the natural conclusion was to distrust the whole tribe of historians. At the same time attempts were made to put historical knowledge on a safer basis by analysing the sources thoroughly and drawing, if possible, on other evidence than that provided by past historians. A sceptical attitude prevailed, but this scepticism did not always imply complete pessimism as to the possi-bility of sound historical knowledge.'
165	
166	Critical minds emphasized how little was known. La Mothe Le Vayer formulated what was to become known as historical Pyrrhonism in his essay of 1668: Du peu de certitude qu'il y a dans l'histoire. R. Simon and Bentley showed to what lengths thorough criticism could go both on sacred and profane history. In 1682 Bayle began to show his hand in the Critique gindrale de 1'histoire du calvinisme, where he declared: "il est bien mal aise de parvenir jusqu'i l'dvidence"; and also: "en un mot, il n'y a point de Filouterie plus grande que celle qui se peut exercer sur les monumens historiques." In the next decades intellectual Europe was overpowered by the massive erudition and searching criticism of the Dictionnaire historique et critique, a best seller, notwithstanding its dimensions. Ernst Cassirer once took Bayle as the proto-type of the modern irudit who has no other concern than the increase of knowledge.2 To contemporaries he was Bayle the sceptic, "l'illustre Bayle qui apprend si bien & douter," as Baron Holbach sympathetically noted.3 His historical Pyrrhonism was most obviously related to his distrust of dogmas and pious beliefs. In another Pyrrhonist, Daniel Huet, the bishop and tutor of the Dauphin, who in 1722 made posthumous scandal by his treatise on the weakness of human understanding, absolute scepticism definitely prevails over scepticism on the subject of historical sources. Two circumstances are relevant here. First Huet had arrived at scepticism by way of his long career of pioneer work in the comparative study of religion, of which the most important product is the Demonstratio evangelica of 1672.4 Secondly, a refuta-tion of his Pyrrhonism, next in importance to the classic one by J. It was only natural that members of religious congregations (Bollandists, Maurists) should make some of the best contributions towards distinguishing between reasonable and unreasonable doubts in history. But the quest for safe historical rules was not confined to them. The discussion on Pyrrhonism raged in German Protestant universities which were just then making their first conspicuous contribution to his torical method. The controversy passed from the hands of historians and philos ophers to those of lawyers, who, being traditionally concerned with the reliability of witnesses, could bring a great deal of experience to bear on this subject. All these people tried to determine the characteristics of what they could call reliable evidence. Books of rhetorical rules on the art of historical writing were of course still produced. The Jesuits wrote a few classic ones of this type (P. Rapin, P. Le Moyne). But a new type of treatise on historical writing developed which broke away from the rhetorical Ars Historica of the Renais-sance and was practically confined to the method of interpreting and criticiz-ing sources. Some text-books were chiefly concerned with textual criticism (authenticity and emendations of texts) : the Ars Critica by J. Le Clerc (1697) is the most important of them. Others, like H. Griffet, Traite des difrfrentes sortes de preuves qui servent i"tablir la verite' de l'histoire (1769) were mainly con-cerned with the historical value of original authorities.

## APPENDIX I1


### John Leland, King's Antiquary

The article on John Leland in the Dictionary of National Biography states (p. 892): "In 1533 Leland was made King's antiquary, an office in which he had neither predecessor nor successor."

The evidence for this statement is not given and, apparently, is not easy to find. The notion that Leland was made King's Antiquary goes back, as far as I can ascertain, to the Life of Camden by T. Smith (169 1) in which one finds this characteristic passage (p. xxvi) :

(Lelandi) industriam perquam laudabilem annua pensione e fisco Regio soluta favore suo fovit Rex Henricus VIII illumque Antiquarii quo merito gloriatus est Lelandus titulo insignivit. Munus istud, quod dolendum est, ab isto tempore omnino desiit: lice t unus et alter (vix enim plures numerantur) superbum illud Historiographi Regii, nescio an satis pro dignitate, nomen sustinuerint.

T. Smith did not quote any evidence, and A. Hall in the Vita Auctoris with which he pre-faced his edition of Leland's Commentarii de scriptoribus britannicis (1709), gave T. Smith as his evidence for the same statement:

ut illum non modo bibliothecae suae praefecit, verum etiam magnifico Antiquarii titulo liberalissime donavit. Unus est inter Anglicae scholae Proceres, virorum eruditorum semper feracissimae, qui ad tanti nominis fastigium conscenderit

#### (b) The Conflict in the Igth Century

Up to the end of the seventeenth century the antiquaries had been left undisturbed in two activities. They had cared for that type of evidence which the ordinary political historian was apt to leave aside; and they had studied those subjects-customs, institutions, art, religion-which were outside the province of the political historian and could be best examined on non-literary evidence. In the early eighteenth century they lost the control of non-literary evidence. The more the "learned" historians accepted the antiquarian's method of checking literary by non-literary evidence, the less the antiquarians could claim numismatics, diplomatics, and epigraphy as their own subjects. 7	# Preface — Disciplining Classics / Altertumswissenschaft als Beruf
8	
9	The articles collected in the present volume explore a few aspects of the role which has been played within the recent history of various kinds of Classical scholarship by three processes of considerable general importance in the sociology of knowledge: disciplinization, institutionalization, and professionalization. To be sure, for certain features of these three processes there were ample pre-modern and early modern partial precedents and parallels, in Europe and elsewhere; but it has been the establishment, the stabilization, and above all the systematic interrelation of all three of them which have so deeply transformed the study of classical antiquity and of other fields over the past several centuries in Europe and America, and more recently in the other parts of the world which have been more or less profoundly influenced by the Western model. Though all three processes are closely related, particularly as they have been put into effect in the past two centuries, nonetheless each term picks out a somewhat different set of features within a complex set of developments and they can be distinguished conceptually.
10	
11	Disciplinization denotes the establishment of a defined field of objects of knowledge and of a set of methods designed to study it in a regulated and inter-subjectively verifiable manner, in such a way as both to create a stable body of information which can be exchanged, examined, and modified synchronically among contemporary researchers on that field and to insure its diachronic transmission to future generations of researchers. Kant’s distinction between a “Wissenschaft” as a systematically interrelated body of knowledge on the one hand and any mere aggregate of unrelated information on the other played a key role in the imposition of disciplinarity upon certain earlier methods of study at the turn of the 19th century and remains enormously, if subliminally, influential. Disciplinization is above all methodological in nature and involves a set of related sub-processes, such as abstraction, formalization, specification, and generalization.
12	
13	Institutionalization refers to the creation of trans-personal organizational systems for the furtherance of specified goals (such as the study of these disciplines) which are taken to be of sufficient importance for society as a whole to justify a substantial financial subvention which will benefit not only in the short term the specific individuals who participate in them but also in the long term an uncertain but presumably larger number of unknown future participants and unknown possible recipients of prospective advantages. Institutionalization secures an at least minimally long-term duration of focused and hence hopefully productive collaboration by distinguishing between functions on the one hand and the individuals who come to fulfill them more or less well and thereby to transform them on the other hand. This is above all an administrative phenomenon and coordinates such sub-processes as legislation, recruitment, career definition, and segmentation.
14	
15	Professionalization, finally, designates the set of transformative processes which individuals are made to undergo so as to make them appear suitable for fulfilling the functions out of which these institutions are composed. Some tribes have rites of passage, others have Promotionen and Habilitationen, dissertations or théses. Before bestowing upon certain already mature adults the reward of a life-long sinecure, society takes a final opportunity to humiliate them by obliging them to fulfil requirements which, however sophisticated their scientific justification, also serve to remind the candidates, who are on the point of joining the bosses, that, however high the value that they themselves may have assigned to their merits, these alone would never have guaranteed them success: the final kick in the pants not only provides an additional impetus for the movement upwards but will also leave psychic bruises which the new boss will alleviate by distributing kicks of his own upon those who are at first only slightly younger than he is. This is above all an anthropological and psychological phenomenon and links with one another procedures of regulation, evaluation, and adjudication, definitions of competence and pertinence, and distinctions between sometimes finely shaded degrees of public and private.
16	
17	The transformation in Classical studies between the end of the 18th and the beginning of the 19th century was one of the most spectacular, successful, and influential of the many processes of scientific modernization which have been determined by these three processes over the past several centuries. The story of the gradual propagation of modern methods and institutions of Classical philology from the seminars of Göttingen in the mid-18th century, through the courses of Friedrich August Wolf at the end of that century, to the establishment of the University of Berlin and the Humanistic Gymnasium in Prussia at the beginning of the next century, and from there (as well as from other sources, including Bavaria) to the rest of Germany, and, with some resistance, to Europe and the world, is a remarkable one. This story usually used to be told (and sometimes still is) in progressivist, unquestioningly positive, indeed occasionally almost hagiographic terms.! Now matters are changing. The crisis in which the field of Classics has found itself for a long time (in some senses, since the beginning) has led to wide-spread confusion, consternation, and complaint, but also, in at least a few cases, to a more sober analysis of the forces which supported and resisted and the mechanisms that rendered possible the transformation to a development which was, precisely, not inevitable and not even very likely. Recent studies of the disciplinization, institutionalization, and professionalization of modern scientific methods in Germany,” England,3 and France‘ have either focused upon the paradigm of Classical philology as a particularly rich and exemplary case or at the very least have important implications for the future study of the history of that field. Wedding the sociology of knowledge to the history of philological method, Pierre Bourdieu to Rudolf Pfeiffer, may tax the imaginative resources of even the most committed interdisciplinarist; but as the fruit from such a union might well issue forth new and more convincing ways of conceiving the history of Classical studies within their social, educational, and scientific contexts.
18	
19	Instead of emphasizing the central steps of the transformation of modern Classical studies in Germany at the turn of the 19th century, which have been studied often (though not definitively), the essays gathered in this volume illuminate certain less familiar aspects of these general trends. A first group of three essays considers some particularly interesting examples of tendencies in pre-modern Classical studies which pointed in certain ways towards later changes but which at the same time indicate the resistances against which the institutionalization of the field had, has had, and has to struggle. A second group of five essays examines the crisis in German Altertumswissenschaft during the last third of the 19th century signalled by the criticisms of Friedrich Nietzsche, and broadens the scope of inquiry to include other developments at the turn of the 20th century. A final group of three essays analyses the question of the disciplinarity of Classics as it is posed in the immediate present and makes suggestions concerning future prospects and challenges. Thus the temporal span of this volume reaches from the 17th century in France to our own days and the foreseeable future. In terms of scholarly disciplines, the emphasis in this, as in the preceding volumes of this series, is upon the university practice of Classical philology; but additional light is thrown upon this field by consideration of related issues in European and American school education, papyrology, and cultural studies, and in the role of philology in the modernization of China. It is particularly worth noting that in this volume, devoted to the professionalization of Classical studies, more than half of the essays have been written by young scholars who stand at the beginning of their own professional careers.
20	
21	This volume is derived from a conference on the subject of the professionalization and institutionalization of philology which was held in conjunction with the Internationales Wissenschaftsforum at Heidelberg University from 2-4 July 1999. As in the previous conferences in this series, which led to the publication of the volumes Collecting Fragments — Fragmente sammeln. Aporemata 1 in 1997, Editing Texts — Texte edieren. Aporemata 2 in 1998, Commentaries — Kommentare. Aporemata 4 in 1999, and Historicization — Historisierung. Aporemata 5 in 2001, the purpose was to explore historical and theoretical aspects of a scholarly practice which has played, and continues to play, an important role in the study of ancient Greece and Rome, as well as of many other cultures. This is the final volume in that series.
22	
23	Although this volume is derived from a conference, it does not simply reproduce the papers presented there: all have been modified, some have been added, others have been omitted. It is hoped that the resulting volume will display even more coherence and unity than the colloquium did, while retaining something of its liveliness and diversity. Besides the authors whose articles are published here, the following scholars also participated in the discussions: Daniel Boyarin (Berkeley), Lorraine Daston (Berlin), Carlotta Dionisotti (London), Luca Giuliani (Munich), Anthony Grafton (Princeton), Andreas Kablitz (Cologne), Stefan Maul (Heidelberg). Funding for this conference, as for all of its predecessors, was provided by a Leibniz prize of the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft; in the present case, additional support was provided by the Fritz Thyssen Stiftung (Cologne) and by the Stiftung Universitét Heidelberg. The staff of the Internationales Wissenschaftsforum, especially Dr. Theresa Reiter and Gudrun Strehlow, were uniformly friendly, helpful, and unruffled. The administrative organization of the conference was carried out with typical patience and inventiveness by Dr. Helga Kohler. The editorial work on this volume, including the preparation of the indices (but not their lemmatization, for which I must take the blame), was performed with grace, skill, and infinite good humor by Ingeborg von Appen; she was assisted in many ways by Dr. Manuel Baumbach and Dagmar Schweinfurth.
24	
25	At the conclusion of this lengthy, intense, and (at least for me personally) highly satisfying project, I would like now once again, and for a last time, to express my heartfelt gratitude to the many students, friends, colleagues, and associates who have been involved in it for their generous and helpful contributions.
26

The motif of improvement completed the familiar trio: “The philosophy or the idealism of our own time can only be perfected by the poetry or the realism of antiquity; and in their mutual interpenetration it will become clear that both, just like mind and body, unity and plurality, are originally one.… The beauty that will spring from the harmony of the ancient and the modern world will be the unity of inner and outer humanity, the revelation of a life that unfolds from the innermost depth and freedom of the spirit.” Conversely, modern “creativity would gradually perish amid mere research unless reawakened and nourished by the exhilarating beauty of Greek art.”91 In short, the philologists who were busy populating the academic landscape with new seminars were setting up a broad front. As for the second factor, replication, Wolfian disciplinary framing persisted even as it was updated, most notably by his star student August Böckh, who went on to teach generations of students at the increasingly prominent University of Berlin. Just like his mentor, Böckh insisted on organicist holism and thus on the inclusion of historical context, a position he defended against proponents of a narrower focus on language and literature. On the whole, the holistic approach prevailed, even as deep language skills continued to be considered the “main key” for unlocking the treasure troves of antiquity.92

Böckh delivered his influential lectures on the “encyclopedia of philology”—the same title Wolf had used—no fewer than twenty-six times between 1809 and 1865. He began by expounding the “concept, scope, and highest purpose of philology.” Albeit universal in nature—as “a renewed recognition and description of all existing human knowledge”—philology must de facto be organized in smaller segments: in keeping with Wolfian doctrine, Böckh preferred separation by time and space—ancient, modern, East/West, Greek, Roman, Hebrew, Indian—over separation by subject, such as language or literature.93

The chosen mode of demarcation meshed well with the nationalist template, making it possible to survey the totality of a people by bundling together all strands of development and approaching them from the center, which was embodied by that people’s spirit: for “it is imperative that we find something common, within which all particulars are contained”; that is, “the principle of a people or era …, the innermost core of its overall being; it cannot be anything else; for anything else would be alien, introduced from the outside.”94

Although the philology of Greece and Rome was in principle one only among many, Böckh deemed it special after all. The completeness of antiquity—finished, distant, and foreign—turned it into a natural unit of engagement, worthy of our attention due to its magnificence and impact: “the philology of classical antiquity is a natural section because the classical is eminently worth knowing and the culture of the Greeks and Romans is the foundation of our entire Bildung.”95

This, according to Böckh, justified elevating the study of Greece and Rome into a kind of paradigm of philology as such: “As we explicitly recognize the other branches of philology as equals, we accept the limitation to classical antiquity, which is pragmatically justified yet coincidental as such, while being aware that it is a limitation. Within that limitation [viz., to classical antiquity], however, we embrace the unlimited concept [viz., of philology], which alone determines method and construction.” Thus, in an elegant squaring of the circle, Greco-Roman philology was one of many philologies yet superior to them. This was as it had to be: after all, understanding Greece and Rome “is no base matter: for it is the understanding of the noblest that the human spirit has produced over thousands of years …; one learns about the entire process of human understanding and of human conditions in an area that is bereft of passion because it lies deep in the past and therefore permits impartial judgment.”96 Böckh expected scholars to devote their efforts to demonstrating connections within the Greco-Roman world—that is, to empirically validate the organicist premise—and to strive for precision even in the smallest matters—“for in philology one must to some extent be pedantic.” Rigorous and immersive engagement cleansed the mind: “Ancient ideas must and can be vividly related to modern thought and have a purifying effect on the latter.” This “purifying effect” issued from superiority: “the poetic works of antiquity are still of higher quality than any others …; there is still no higher spirit than that which pervaded antiquity.” By conveying “noble and majestic matters,” antiquity supplied “truly human, impartial, intellectual … views and makes people free and liberal.”97

Except for the explicit downgrading of other cultures, all the principal elements of the Wolfian agenda were thus faithfully preserved and energetically disseminated for another sixty years: the presumption of organic national unity, which called for scholarship to recover it; exacting attention to detail; and the superior quality of that specific subject that promised personal improvement.98

The customary claim to purity received attention in Böckh’s address to a convention of German philologists, schoolteachers, and orientalists (in that presumably hierarchical sequence) in 1850. Conceding certain “points of contact” between “oriental and classical peoples” and even musing that “a comparative cultural history of all of antiquity might eventually turn out to be the principal objective of philological science,” he reminded his audience that “confessors of classical philology”—note the religious phrasing—dealt with a people “in which a purely national culture had fully formed that was as independent from foreign influences as possible, and that as swiftly as possible transformed all foreign elements it had absorbed into its own being and its own flesh and blood.”99

In

the end,

there was no meaningful bridge

to be built: compartmentalization ruled supreme, and hierarchies among cultures were not to be doubted. The averred primacy of Greece and Rome did not even allow for genuine historicism. It thus hardly mattered that Böckh sought to replace his “master” Wolf’s proposed formal organization of the field with his own scheme. The “science” of an essentialized, nationalized Greco-Roman antiquity was confirmed as the basic (and pivotal) unit of study, blocking any hope of cross-cultural history.100

### Manufacturing an Academic-Pedagogical Complex

Before we move on to the third pillar of success—political power—let us very briefly take stock of the new rules of the game. The complete toolbox was now in place. Greeks were on top, especially Athenians, and at any rate Greeks before the age of Alexander the Great, when they were still classical and pure. Wolf, in Gibbonian fashion, had laid claim to the Byzantine period as well—and rightly so, given that its fusion of Greek and Roman ought to have been every classicist’s wet dream. Yet that was not to be, just as the logic of the purist-nationalist model (coupled more specifically with apprehension about Greeks mingling with “Orientals”) militated against full inclusion of the yet-to-be conceptualized “Hellenistic” period.101 Under such constraints, other cultures, even neighboring ones, were out; so were Christian Greeks and Romans. While imitation of the ancients was passé, meticulous study had become de rigueur: as “scientific” and comprehensive as possible, it had to be both specialized and holistic at once, which inevitably turned out to be impossible. It had to prioritize scholarship at the expense of pedagogy yet fill teaching positions in secondary schools with its products, with predictable consequences. No matter: this study was not only valued in and of itself but also meant to improve the student.
