23:Even though my survey is necessarily highly selective (or even reductive, not to mention disrespectful), my main point should not be controversial: that over the last 250 years, academic ideals and practices have made it ever harder for us to explore, understand, and publicize our shared foundational history. In an apparent paradox, these trends gained momentum just as spectacular advances in the decipherment of ancient scripts and languages together with the rise of archaeological fieldwork made such a foundational history feasible for the first time.
111:In his telling, the origins of this cultural miracle were ostensibly more complex than Winckelmann had allowed for, rooted in a mixture of Phoenician and Egyptian modes of thought—a remnant of what Martin Bernal labeled the “Oriental model” that credited them with foundational influences on Greek development. But Herder took pains to undercut it straight away: “I consider it undeniable that Greece received seeds of culture, language, arts, and sciences from elsewhere, and this can clearly be shown for some areas—sculpture, architecture, mythology, literature. But that the Greeks might just as well not have received all that, that they gave all that an entirely new character, so that in every way the ‘beautiful,’ in the true sense of the word, was without doubt their own creation.… Nothing Oriental, Phoenician, and Egyptian retained its nature: it became Greek and in some ways they [i.e., the Greeks] were almost too much originals who re-dressed and dressed up everything according to their own nature.”26
167:One could not ask for a clearer expression of the foundational principle of the field: language and literature were to enjoy primacy over art and archaeology. The formative “images” Heyne invokes were not visuals of actual objects but figurative images conveyed by the writings of premier Greek authors. No matter how wide the scope of remains marshalled to access the ancient spirit, there was no path to a proper appreciation of Greece (or Rome) other than prior immersion in and mastery of language and literature. Holistic as the field was supposed to be, not all its elements were created equal. That premise—conveniently exemplified in Heyne’s reading by none less than the pioneer of ancient art history himself—has lingered ever since.42
495:Yet neither one of these options encouraged spatial or temporal broadening. Altertumswissenschaft embraced closedness as a foundational principle. Meanwhile, History as a field was profoundly shaped by what Sebastian Conrad has called the “two ‘birth defects’ of the modern sciences and humanities [that] hinder our ability to achieve a systematic grasp of processes that span the world,” namely fixation on the nation state and Eurocentrism.161
587:But when Wilamowitz in 1921 reiterated the foundational vision of the field, he not only abandoned its claim to superiority as a thing of the past and gave up on strict demarcations but also found himself compelled to recognize new disciplinary divisions, if only as a sign of human weakness. “Philology—which is still called classical even though it no longer claims the primacy that this epithet implies—is defined by its subject matter, Greco-Roman culture in its essence and in every expression of its existence. This civilization is a single whole, even if it may not be possible precisely to define when it began and ended. It is the task of classical scholarship to bring that past existence back to life by the power of scholarship.… Because the life we strive to fathom is a single whole, our science too is a single whole. Its division into the disciplines of philology, ancient history, epigraphy, numismatics, and latterly also papyrology can be justified only with the limitations of human capacity and even in the specialist must not smother awareness of the whole.”195
711:Changing track might seem like a revolution but is merely a restoration: a move to put the past back together again. The intellectual imperative for restoration foundational developments were If (increasingly) global in scale, why hack them into little pieces and box them up? How can we hope to understand them if we do that? And why would we choose to imagine that “Ancient History” somehow “belonged” to the ancient Greeks and Romans, perhaps with some of their neighbors thrown in to soften the edges?
737:This does not merely apply to parts of the world that have been as heavily transformed by recent immigration flows as North America: the need for inclusionary ancient history must not be misconstrued as a quintessentially American concern, only to be dismissed elsewhere. Even if other societies wished to lay claim to (comparatively) more cohesive or restricted foundational pasts, they would nevertheless be unable to escape a world that has become increasingly interconnected and globalized. In that regard, we are indeed “all Americans now,” as Le Monde proclaimed after 9/11. Understanding our shared roots has become more important than ever. The foundational history model actively promotes that aspiration, taking us a step closer to what Sebastian Conrad calls “the utopian promise of global history: to turn us into citizens of the world.”4
743:There is no denying a simple fact: global ancient history, conceived of as foundational history, is “our” ancient history, whoever and wherever we are. Just as we all share African roots, all of us are now the heirs, or captives, of that global ancient history, of the world it created. There is no other kind.
809:Giving short(er) shrift to temporal connectivity represents a loss: since that dimension, much of what historians do acknowledging the globalizing qualities of such work would boost the standing of global history. Just as with contextualization, this approach benefits from explicit problematization. For any given case, it is just as challenging to account for the impact of temporal transfers as for those of a spatial nature. Any periodization, including the concept of “foundational history,” is predicated on shifts in the balance of continuities and discontinuities over time.
861:Comparative history allows us to critique “local” explanations derived from and for a single case by contrasting inputs and outcomes in other cases. This matters especially whenever “local” explanations are tied up with notions of specialist expertise and mastery. Grew captures this poignantly: “Whereas concern for detailed accuracy can bury significance under trivia, comparison can make the apparently trivial significant—an asset few of us can afford to ignore.”42 Historians should embrace all of these payoffs regardless of their subject matter. But comparison plays an even greater role in the foundational history approach to global ancient world studies that I outlined in the opening chapter: its typological-developmental perspective all but requires systematic comparison across the globe.
923:At its most basic, world history may simply offer parallel exposition of regional developments in different parts of the planet. In practice, it tends to be structured by the search for unifying elements, for common or contrasting trajectories and dynamics. Much as in the more ambitious versions of comparative history, its greatest promise lies in approaches that focus on features, concepts, and processes and track them across cases regardless of whether those cases were connected at the time. This makes world history particularly suitable for covering phenomena that emerged multiply and independently around the globe, such as those that define the foundational phase of sociocultural evolution described in the opening chapter. This preoccupation with typological and developmental patterns and the widest possible spatiotemporal scope: the more cases we capture, the more robust assessments can be.68
929:For recent periods, when networks finally extended across the entire planet, “world history” has increasingly been absorbed by “global history,” which is commonly defined by its emphasis on connectivity. That, however, is not an issue for students of the premodern world. In fact, while global in scope, foundational history is concerned precisely with the phase of maximum disconnection, after the Holocene had severed the Americas from Afroeurasia but prior to the modern Atlantic exchange.69
939:This matters a lot for the foundational history project. Both comparative and (genuine) world history are essential means of overcoming the limitations of absolute chronology and connectivity, both of which tend to exclude the Americas and large parts of Africa from global ancient world studies. Yet just as “world histories” of antiquity commonly give short shrift to those parts of the globe, comparative studies that juxtapose Afroeurasia and the preconquest Americas have also remained rare, even as we finally observe an uptick in interest. This is one of the biggest potential growth areas for a globalized ancient history.75
943:The intrinsic properties of different approaches are not the only factor that determines their appeal or chances of success. Academic traditions, incentive structures, and support systems matter just as much. As we will see in the remainder of this chapter, relaxation of conventional ideals of mastery and the promotion of collaborative efforts are of paramount importance for bolstering work that moves beyond basic framing or exploration of connections toward more systematically comparative or planetary perspectives. In the final analysis, the latter two are not merely more challenging—whether in terms of method (comparison) or data volume and variety (planetary scale). They are also the ones most likely to advance the globalization of ancient studies, and thus to make the concept of foundational history a reality. If we want to put our understanding of the ancient world on a more solid footing, it is those approaches that will require the greatest attention and investment.
945:### Who Is Afraid of Foundational History?
1027:Every step of the way—from undergraduate theses, admission to graduate programs, graduate instruction, and credentialing based on “masterpieces” (aka dissertations) to hiring, renewal, tenure, and promotion —the academic humanities doggedly adhere to a model that undermines cross-cultural and multidisciplinary engagement. True “foundational history” is all but impossible under these circumstances: feasible perhaps at some levels of teaching but hardly in advanced training or research.82
1045:The foundational history agenda contends with a self-enforcing system of deterrence. The lack of systemic opportunity and incentive, of instructional models, and of consensual standards all feed off each other, preventing alternatives from gaining traction. Formidable as it is, however, that negative feedback loop is only part of a bigger story. As though the lack of incentives for change were not enough, meaningful reform faces further obstacles.
1055:IN THE ANGLOSPHERE, the continued existence of Classics as an academic field endowed with its own institutional units and degree programs is one of the biggest impediments to the development of a foundational history that does justice to the full sweep of the human journey. Its presence deepens the fractures created by the manner in which past generations of European scholars responded to the accelerating expansion of new knowledge about ancient cultures beyond Greece and Rome: instead of nurturing and accommodating flexibly comprehensive domain of studying and understanding the ancient world, an ever-larger number of ever-narrower niche fields were spun off to populate the academic landscape while hard lines were drawn both between white Europe and everywhere else and between literate and nonliterate societies.
1071:Second, in a considerable number of academic institutions, Classics partly or entirely absorbs the study and teaching of the history of the Greco-Roman world, an area that thanks to its rich documentation and exceptionally deep scholarly penetration will always be an essential element of any global foundational history. By laying claim to this essential element, Classics isolates and detaches it from the study of other ancient histories as well as from intellectual currents in the History profession at large. Both of these barriers interfere with globalizing perspectives.
1105:As we will see, the distinction between content and template is vital, if often elided, especially but not only in conservative interventions. It should be perfectly obvious that no meaningful engagement with foundational history is possible without Greece and Rome. The same is true of any globalized version of art history, comparative literature, or philosophy. At the same time, it is by no means obvious that the concept and the established practice of Classics as an academic field are somehow required, or at least desirable or helpful, to ensure a strong presence of the Greco-Roman world in any such endeavors.
1261:At which point will scholars who engage with various aspects of the Greco-Roman world and its varied afterlives no longer have enough in common to share an academic home and be better off elsewhere? By challenging foundational tenets of Classics such as Western exceptionalism and exclusionary requirements that curtail access, a genuinely decolonizing agenda can only bring us closer to that point. It is more likely to dissolve the field than to save it.
1321:Are we still talking about Classics as a field centered on Greece and Rome, or have we already left it behind in favor of cross-cultural engagement with foundational traditions? The survivalist impulse muddies the waters, obscuring the fact that tough choices about the reorganization of teaching and research would have to be made.
1395:That said, although the dismantling of Classics as a field will remove a big obstacle to those future developments, it will not by itself bring them about. Much hinges on the question of how global ancient or foundational history can be organized and institutionalized. History programs tend to marginalize even practitioners of Greco-Roman ancient history, and for the most part restrict engagement with any other parts of the ancient world to the shallowest of introductory world history surveys.
1399:Even so, Classics and cognate programs bear only part of the blame. The demotion of the more distant past also stems from a more general tendency, that of focusing research and (perhaps especially) teaching on more recent periods of history that can be more readily and more directly connected to current conditions. Such presentist undercurrents can never be fully eliminated, nor should they be. It is perfectly reasonable to turn to whatever history promises to throw the most light on the roads that were taken (or not taken) in making our world, and on what was lost in the process. Ancient historians must mobilize this curiosity for their own purposes by making the strongest possible case for the profound relevance of their subject matter for understanding the present. This, of course, is the whole point of reframing “ancient” history as “foundational” history.
1403:And while other national traditions may differ in specific ways, these problems tend to be widespread. The disappearance of the model of Altertumswissenschaft from continental Europe has generally failed to promote more inclusive ancient studies. Thus, while the dismantling of Classics is a necessary precondition for establishing a viable field of planetary foundational history, it is clearly not sufficient.

Any global approach to the past today grapples with the same issues as these Göttingen professors had done. Instead of recovering from a multigenerational hiatus, as it has only recently managed to do, debate could have taken off in earnest more than 200 years ago, shaping modern historiography in fruitful and unexpected ways.12
59:And that was only the start: in Gatterer’s days, there was no way of anticipating just how nationalist and racist much of nineteenth-century academia would become. Despite its name, instruction went well beyond Greek and Latin to include religion, pedagogy, history, geography, mathematics, astronomy, and natural sciences. The new model spread, initially replicated by alumni or other former members of the Göttingen seminar and before long through imitation by others. Founders generally managed to copy the practice of obtaining state funding for positions, stipends, and other resources.44

277:That narrowing and fusing went hand in hand with exclusion of the Hebrew tradition, downgraded to that of an uncultured people, and even of the New Testament. Wolf at one point deemed the latter to have resulted from Jewish recognition and embrace of Greek superiority that resulted in a text of “Greek morals, mixed with Jewish ideas,” composed in Greek that was “revolting” and “barbaric …, full of Hebraisms and Judaizing turns of phrase.”77
279:While Wolf’s banishment of early Judaism from his new field arguably reflected his desire to rid the study of antiquity from the influence of theology, such rhetoric went far beyond what might have been required to achieve this goal. Endowed with a well-known language and literature, the ancient Hebrews more than any other culture had to be cut down to size in order to justify the separatist elevation of GreeceandRome. There is some bitter irony in the fact that all of this took place at the University of Halle, where August Hermann Francke in the opening years of the eighteenth century had established not only a conventional pedagogical seminar for the teaching of Greek and Latin but also a high-profile collegium orientale theologicum for the study of biblical and rabbinical Hebrew, Aramaic, Samaritan, Syriac, Arabic, and Ethiopian.78
281:For Wolf himself, the hardening of the GreeceandRome template required rejection of comparative questions—an implicit repudiation of his own earlier comparative work on Greek and biblical philology for his masterpiece Prolegomena ad Homerum of 1795. Disciplinization demanded self-disciplining.79
285:However the discipline’s many branches were to be configured, language skills were always central. Wolf made sure to impress this on his students, not just future scholars in the seminar but also his more diverse lecture audience: “We can never fully get to know the true state of a nation without reading its authors in the original. For language represents a key element of the state of a nation and belongs to the whole, which the study of antiquity searches for.”81
295:This particular “metaphysical castle in the air”—GreeceandRome—had been built to last; and last it did. Wolf’s exposition proved to be paradigmatic, not so much because of the published version of 1807 (in an obscure and short-lived journal he had founded for the occasion) but because of the reach and success of his lectures, which had already spawned epigonal publications by members of the audience.86
297:Yet even the lectures, popular as they were, were just opium for the masses. It was Wolf’s seminar that created future professionals, and was thus the main source of his impact. Its members were an elite group, as only the most gifted were able to join (and often received stipends). Students were barred from belonging to more than one seminar, a restriction that encouraged specialization and discipline formation. According to one contemporary observer, seminarists signaled their commitment not merely by “slavish studying” but by adopting a dress code so distinctive that it made them recognizable from far away. Those were the shock troops charged with conquering the true antiquity.87
299:The Prussian government had approved the establishment of the seminar on the understanding that a good teacher would benefit from research skills. To this end, the curriculum was supposed to cover “interpretation” (i.e., lexicography, grammar, and textual criticism) and “disputation” (based on written homework on topics often bereft of relevance for later teaching careers) as well as “pedagogy.” Wolf, however, prioritized the first two to the extent that the third was even omitted from his own outline of the seminar rules. Producing research papers was to be a central element of the philologist’s training. Foregrounding research at the expense of pedagogical preparation while upholding the strict disciplinary boundaries that Wolf had set out in his exposition, this template was adopted across the philology seminars of the nineteenth century. What is more, this seminar praxis helped shape the modus operandi of the entire university.88
301:What accounts for the success of this type of seminar and the rigorous approach to the study of Greece and Rome that it promoted? The reasons lie in a mixture of zeitgeist—others held similar views; replication—via academic genealogies; and political power—which allowed a particular vision to capture the relevant institutions. I briefly touch on all three in turn. Friedrich Ast, founder of the philological seminar in Landshut in Bavaria the nineteenth century, provides a striking the beginning of at contemporaneous to Wolf’s. Comprehensiveness was a key element of Ast’s program: “Philology is the study of the classical world in its complete artistic, scientific, public and peculiar existence. The center of this study is the spirit of antiquity, which is reflected most purely in the works of ancient authors, but is likewise reflected in the outer and peculiar life of the classical peoples.… Only the harmonious fusion of all elements of Alterthumswissenschaft can bring forth true philology, because only the comprehensive appreciation and understanding of antiquity reveals the spirit of the classical world.”89
311:The motif of improvement completed the familiar trio: “The philosophy or the idealism of our own time can only be perfected by the poetry or the realism of antiquity; and in their mutual interpenetration it will become clear that both, just like mind and body, unity and plurality, are originally one.… The beauty that will spring from the harmony of the ancient and the modern world will be the unity of inner and outer humanity, the revelation of a life that unfolds from the innermost depth and freedom of the spirit.” Conversely, modern “creativity would gradually perish amid mere research unless reawakened and nourished by the exhilarating beauty of Greek art.”91 In short, the philologists who were busy populating the academic landscape with new seminars were setting up a broad front. As for the second factor, replication, Wolfian disciplinary framing persisted even as it was updated, most notably by his star student August Böckh, who went on to teach generations of students at the increasingly prominent University of Berlin. Just like his mentor, Böckh insisted on organicist holism and thus on the inclusion of historical context, a position he defended against proponents of a narrower focus on language and literature. On the whole, the holistic approach prevailed, even as deep language skills continued to be considered the “main key” for unlocking the treasure troves of antiquity.92
313:Böckh delivered his influential lectures on the “encyclopedia of philology”—the same title Wolf had used—no fewer than twenty-six times between 1809 and 1865. He began by expounding the “concept, scope, and highest purpose of philology.” Albeit universal in nature—as “a renewed recognition and description of all existing human knowledge”—philology must de facto be organized in smaller segments: in keeping with Wolfian doctrine, Böckh preferred separation by time and space—ancient, modern, East/West, Greek, Roman, Hebrew, Indian—over separation by subject, such as language or literature.93

=== WILAMOWITZ/Mommsen in Scheidel ===
381:No matter: mission creep proved unstoppable. Like a cancer, lofty norms designed for small elite seminars spread into the wider world of secondary education. Critically, schoolmen at prominent places, who were themselves among the most successful products of those seminars, keenly embraced this implausible agenda. Inevitably defeated by the mismatch between expectations and feasibility, instruction turned into drilling grammar instead of self-improvement, serving credentialing instead of transformative engagement. As Friedrich Nietzsche, Germany’s most famous philology dropout, satirized the situation, the philologist “teaches cramming.”122
505:Even so, the latter model became increasingly unstable. Over time, Altertumswissenschaft differentiated into branches that strained against the overarching template: dedicated chairs for Classical Archaeology and Ancient History began to appear in the 1840s and 1860s, respectively. The advance of compartmentalization fed on the expansion of funding and enrollment in the late nineteenth century, precipitating the separation of Greek from Latin philology and, around the turn of the century, leading to the creation of the first chairs for Byzantine Studies and medieval Latin. This process proved unstoppable as ever more stringent norms of professionalism took hold, undermining an organicist ideal of unity that even as it was nominally upheld was being dismantled in practice.166 However, while classical philology and archaeology managed to acquire clear profiles as fields that dealt with texts or artifacts, Greco-Roman “Ancient History” remained less well defined: its single most famous practitioner, Theodor Mommsen, did not even consider it a meaningful academic field. Reflecting this ambiguity, there was no obvious home for the twenty-one Ancient History chairs created between 1869 and 1904: sometimes they were attached to Altertumswissenschaft and sometimes they were not. The one thing that united them was a hardened commitment to Greece and Rome and exclusion of everything else.167
547:In Germany itself, meanwhile, efforts either to preserve a unitary Altertumswissenschaft or to open “Ancient History” to ancient Egypt and West Asia both failed. Just as in the late eighteenth century Göttingen had been an incubator of initiatives that pulled historians in wildly different directions—exemplified by Heyne, Gatterer, and Meiners—around 1900 the University of Berlin played the same role, this time with the classical philologist Ulrich von Wilamowitz-Moellendorff and the ancient historian Eduard Meyer taking the lead.
549:In a nod to the Wolfian vision, Wilamowitz labored to create a unified institute for all matters Greek and Roman. For some time, Berlin’s Greco-Roman historians had run their own institute alongside the original philology seminar. They were coopted into the latter by 1907, followed five this later by classical archaeology. Wilamowitz considered years arrangement “perfect, in some sense a model.” Nonetheless, the study of both ancient history and archaeology had reached such a degree of independence that this (re)unification was more apparent than real. Likewise, classical philology—now more modestly defined as the study of Greek and Latin language and literature—had already begun to be accepted as a separate discipline. Altertumswissenschaft had irremediably fractured and no amount of organizational legerdemain could turn back the clock.181
557:Most importantly for the issue at hand, Meyer drew a contrast between history and philology, expressly rejecting Wolfian conceptualization: when it comes to the study of antiquity, “the amalgamation of both, their merger under the heading of ‘Altertumswissenschaft,’ is unjustified and confusing, and has become quite detrimental to the treatment of ancient history. This has artificially promoted the shredding of what belongs together and the isolation of particular elements of a field, as well as specialization and the much-hyped academic division of labor, on which our era prides itself as much as any people or any person can pride themselves on their weaknesses. The history of antiquity is and must never be anything other than part of a single, general history, and both parties—ancient and modern historical research—must never forget that.” Meyer consequently criticized the fact that in some universities, ancient historians were not based in historical seminars (alongside practitioners of modern history) but lumped together with philologists in units devoted to Altertumswissenschaft—a transparent criticism of his colleague Wilamowitz’s reorganization of their Berlin institute.186
559:In addition to resistance rooted in the hardening of disciplinary boundaries and traditional preference for pairing Greece and Rome, Meyer’s initiative encountered three major problems. Feasibility was one of them: only a polymath could hope to master all the necessary skills. Then again, for true experts even that would never be good enough: even though back in the gymnasium Meyer had translated the notoriously challenging Latin author Tacitus into Greek, Wilamowitz nevertheless doubted his control of the minutiae of Greek alongside his command of specialized scholarship. The second problem was that Meyer’s approach ran counter to the zeitgeist of the first half of the twentieth century, which drove nationalism to unprecedented heights.187
585:Wilamowitz stood ready to engage dissenters. In a speech in 1892, he acknowledged the separation of history from philology for the study of the more recent past but warned against following this example for Greco-Roman antiquity itself: even if genuine breadth was impractical in actual scholarship, “this holistic vision remains the ideal demand of scholarship.” Thus, he insisted, we must reject “the desire for emancipation”—note the term!—among certain historians and archaeologists who wished to imitate their peers who dealt with later periods in abandoning the study and teaching of ancient languages; for this could only invalidate their own work. “Ancient History” was to be kept on a tight leash.194
587:But when Wilamowitz in 1921 reiterated the foundational vision of the field, he not only abandoned its claim to superiority as a thing of the past and gave up on strict demarcations but also found himself compelled to recognize new disciplinary divisions, if only as a sign of human weakness. “Philology—which is still called classical even though it no longer claims the primacy that this epithet implies—is defined by its subject matter, Greco-Roman culture in its essence and in every expression of its existence. This civilization is a single whole, even if it may not be possible precisely to define when it began and ended. It is the task of classical scholarship to bring that past existence back to life by the power of scholarship.… Because the life we strive to fathom is a single whole, our science too is a single whole. Its division into the disciplines of philology, ancient history, epigraphy, numismatics, and latterly also papyrology can be justified only with the limitations of human capacity and even in the specialist must not smother awareness of the whole.”195
589:By then unitary holism had fully devolved into a purely notional ideal, no longer applied in academic practice. And even that ideal was effectively called into question by Wilamowitz’s reference to the barriers that had fallen—between Greece and Rome and Asia and Egypt, between “classical and Christian philology and archaeology,” between Greek and Latin and Arabic and Syriac. Yet even as this newly permeable field could no longer claim to be either classical or classicizing, it somehow remained an identifiable “living whole.” It is unclear how all these disparate elements were to be reconciled: the center simply could not hold. In an address in 1900, Wilamowitz himself had already admitted that “antiquity as a unit and as an ideal are gone; scholarship itself has destroyed this belief.”196
591:In his memorial speech on Wilamowitz, his Berlin successor Werner Jaeger addressed the tension between idealism and historicism: “Two souls continuously struggled in his chest: the historian, who only wants to know what happened, and the humanist and philologist, who must worship and proclaim what is great and eternal.” Yet what was true of Wilamowitz remains true of the field itself: these tensions endure wherever a version of Altertumswissenschaft has survived, most notably in the Anglosphere’s Classics.197
595:The “Western Civ” route offered one way out. No longer meant to enable communion with the ideal, the study of Greece and Rome could also be legitimated as a way of getting to know the cradle of “our” (“Western”) civilization. Once again, Wilamowitz entered the fray. At a major convention for secondary school education in 1900, he laid out the strategy. A century ago, he said, antiquity had been held up as an ideal and was supposed to be studied for that reason. “Now we have convinced ourselves that that was an error.” We had come to understand “instead” (!) that we had close ties to that period, which could still be approached as “a historical unit.” While outright idealization was passé, Greece and Rome were still of great value as the distant progenitors of the present. This perspective called for greater breadth: Paul became as important as Plato, and classical Greece might even have to take a back seat to the Hellenistic period that shaped the Roman empire and early Christianity (and thereby had the biggest impact on the present).199
597:Wilamowitz went all in: European civilization was not merely based on Greece; it was in a sense still Greek. “This is what we want to tell people: all of you, whichever nation you belong to, as long as you are civilized peoples, share the same foundation”—that was “what ties us together, that the world is one, because it rests on the same culture, just as it is governed by the same God.” Greco-Roman “world culture” was “not only the foundation but also as it were a version of our own, and that [ancient world culture] is Greek, since all of Roman civilization was merely an integrating province thereof.” Scholars must therefore convince their students that the lineages of all aspects of our thinking “lead directly to Hellas.” The Greeks were “the ancestors of all modern civilized peoples.”200
613:Although the contemporary legacies and influences of Greece and Rome of by been routinely had Altertumswissenschaft, to antiquity’s role as an ideal object of study and its purifying effects. As the latter went out of fashion, the former needed to be played up, just as Wilamowitz sought to do.202
629:Whether in the United States or elsewhere, however, this approach could not hope to satisfy Wilamowitz’s demand for deep immersion. Greece and Rome, and their “Ancient History” along with them, had been turned into a distant antechamber of the present, only opportunistically connected to its immediate neighbors and strictly cut off from other parts of the ancient world. At the same time, the idealization model showed considerable staying power despite its growing irrelevance to public discourse. In Germany itself, Wilamowitz’s push did not lead anywhere. Just a few years earlier Jacob Burckhardt had still the “free …, original, and identified spontaneous” Greeks “as the brilliant people of the world.” More importantly, Wilamowitz failed to convince conservative schoolteachers, committed to the ideal of the “classical,” of the need to embrace postclassical sources and the New Testament. The latter had been rejected as a philological school text as far back as Heyne. The classicizing idealist template had been hammered into too many heads for too long, and had been faithfully reproduced for too many generations.205
633:At the same time, the “third humanism”—that is, neo-neohumanism—of Werner Jaeger, Wilamowitz’s successor in Berlin, appealed to the exact same principles. In his Paideia of 1933, Jaeger stressed that there was no history of the whole planet, only histories of clusters. The European cluster was rooted in the Greeks, who, unique in being endowed with “culture” as a “conscious ideal,” ensured the special character of the West. The Greeks owed their special position not merely to the “affinity of racial kinship, however important especially that factor is for the inner understanding of another people”—Berve would have approved—but also to the “fateful spiritual connection” established by enduring cultural legacies. The implication is clear: since no people can be valued more highly than the Greeks, and thus also those associated with them, others must by definition be inferior.207
1141:As immersion in the study of Greece and Rome was thought to improve the mind in ways no other subjects could, Classics became a marker of prestige not just for the subject matter but also for those who were familiar with it. The enduring application of the term “classical” to matters Greek and Roman serves as a reminder that the shift from emulation and idealization to professionalized study has remained incomplete. Yet even the venerable Ulrich von Wilamowitz-Moellendorff detested it: “I have never been able to make anything of the word ‘classical,’ which is an abomination to me.”20

2. 根据另一种理论，历史主义的危机根植于尼采对历史主义背后价值与文化的批判，相关内容集中表现在《不合时宜的沉思》（1873）的第二篇论文《历史对于人生的利弊》之中。尼采控诉历史主义的本质在于历史主义对历史的兴趣偏离了生存的真正问题：我们获得的所有有关过去、关于他人行为的全部知识，都无法决定我们应当如何生活。尼采的论述在当时只激起很少的反应，但在战后一代中他的思想变得越来越重要且受到高度评价。

参见Jaeger and Rüsen, Geschichte, pp.141—146。

3. 另一种理论指出，历史主义的危机肇端于19世纪90年代卡尔·兰普雷希特《德国史》（1891—1909）的出版，该著作推动了基于自然科学的历史观。兰普雷希特主张史学应当确定普遍的因果律，如同自然科学所做的那样。为了替自己的方法论辩护，兰普雷希特向威廉时代最重要的历史学家（弗里德里希·梅尼克，马克斯·德尔布吕克，奥托·欣策，马克斯·伦茨，赫尔曼·昂肯，格奥尔格·冯·贝娄）的方法论提出了挑战，而这些人都成长于兰克学派的传统之内。结果这导致了兰普雷希特和冯·贝娄间激烈的辩论，史称“兰普雷希特之争”。据说，这场辩论使得历史主义者失去了对于自身方法论的信心。

例如，参见Bambach, Heidegger, Dilthey and the Crisis of Historicism (Ithaca: Cornell University Press, 1995), pp. 1—20; Iggers, German Conception of History, pp.128—129; and Meinecke, “Von der Krisis des Historismus” , in Werke IV, pp.200—201。

4. 还有一种理论认为历史主义的危机表现在对历史中意义、结构和进步信任的缺失。这一崩塌是第一次世界大战所带来的创伤的一部分，人们普遍意识到数百万年轻生命白白牺牲。历史主义者在战前对历史的进步性抱有极深的信任。那些代表性的历史主义者—德罗伊森、特洛尔奇和梅尼克—都是自由派民族主义分子，他们坚信强大的中央集权德国国家的价值将引领历史走上更加自由、平等和幸福的道路。然而德国现实的战争行为完全破坏了这一信念。国家并没有带领德意志民族朝着自由和幸福迈进，而是出于站不住脚的理由杀戮了整整一代人。

例如Iggers, German Conception of History, pp.124, 133, 141, 143。

5. 根据最后一种理论，历史主义的危机来自自身内部的矛盾，其中有一点特别突出：对于客观知识的理想与历史强作用力的信念之间的冲突。历史主义者的科学观和目标假定了以自然科学为模板的客观知识理想，似乎历史学家能完全超脱价值与成见保持中立。但是历史主义自身证明了这样的知识理想太天真了。其中的矛盾非常明显：如果一切人类立场都取决于历史与文化条件，那么历史学家怎么可能书写客观的、毫无偏见的历史？

上述哪种理论正确？所有理论都有对错。它们的正确之处在于共同指向历史主义传统中包含的实际问题；它们的错误之处在于无法解释历史主义传统的消逝。所有这些有关历史主义危机的叙述都暗含了一个假设，即历史主义的消逝是由于其深层悲剧性的缺陷或矛盾。但如我们所见的那样，思想家们没有就此缺陷或矛盾取得一致意见；哪怕有这样的一致意见，我们也没理由确信历史主义的消逝与之相关。毕竟，什么时候一场思想运动会单单因为思想或理论上的难点而偃旗息鼓呢？

不过，历史主义的衰落有一个更为简明的解释。这里我们只需回想起历史主义的原初任务：使历史学被承认是一门科学。在实现这一目标的尝试中，历史主义者取得了惊人的成功，至少史学在大学中成为自主的专业，是被认可具有自然科学相同特权的学术主体。对此有所怀疑的人们只需回想一下自18世纪中期以来德国学术体系中史学地位惊人的提升即可。所以历史主义式微的原因非常简单：历史主义已经达成了它设定的目标，不再需要继续存在下去。根据这一观点，历史主义并不是凄惨地落败而是取得异常的成功。历史主义继续发挥着深远影响，它从不会真正逝去。它继续在所有人之内存活着，今天我们作为梅尼克革命的继承者，公正地来讲都是历史主义者。

It was organized in learned societies instead of being centred in the universities; it was fostered by gentlemen rather than by schoolmasters. They preferred travel to the emendation of texts and altogether subordinated literary texts to coins, statues, vases and inscriptions. Addison discussed the relevance of coins to literary studies,' and Gibbon, who had taken leave of Oxford, renewed his education by spending twenty pounds on the twenty volumes of the Memoirs of the Academy of Inscriptions. Italy was still the centre of attraction, both for the learned and the curious. But it was a more complex Italy, where Etruscan antiquities counted hardly less than Roman ruins, and where extraordinary discoveries began to be announced, from Herculaneum in 1736 and from Pompeii in 1748. Furthermore the antiquities of Greece were growing in significance both for the lucky few-chiefly Englishmen and Frenchmen-who could visit them,'and for the larger, but still restricted number who could afford to buy the splendid books in which they were illustrated: primarily the Antiquities of Athens by Stuart and Revett (1762).

387:Up to the end of the seventeenth century the antiquaries had been left undisturbed in two activities. They had cared for that type of evidence which the ordinary political historian was apt to leave aside; and they had studied those subjects-customs, institutions, art, religion-which were outside the province of the political historian and could be best examined on non-literary evidence. In the early eighteenth century they lost the control of non-literary evidence. The more the "learned" historians accepted the antiquarian's method of checking literary by non-literary evidence, the less the antiquarians could claim numismatics, diplomatics, and epigraphy as their own subjects. But they remained the teachers of the four antiquitates-publicae, privatae, sacrae, militares. The right of the antiquarians to exist was not challenged in the eighteenth century. The "philosophic" historians had no use for their erudition and did not try to direct it to new channels. The question changed its aspect and became a more definite challenge to the antiquarians when, towards the end of the century, it became evident (thanks chiefly to Winckelmann and Gibbon) that erudition and philosophy were not incompatible. The combination of philosophic history with the antiquarian's method of research became the aim which many of the best historians of the nineteenth century proposed to themselves. It is still the aim that many of us propose to ourselves. It means two difficult things: the constant repression of the a priori attitude inherent in the generalizing approach of the philosophic historian and, on the other hand, the avoidance of the antiquarian mentality with its fondness for classification and for irrelevant detail. The antiquary was a connoisseur and an enthusiast; his world was static, his ideal was the collection. Whether he was a dilettante or a professor, he lived to classify. In certain cases his habits of mind were reinforced by the methods obtaining in subjects with which he was closely connected. Antiquitates sacrae bordered on theological territories; antiquitates publicae were hardly distinguishable, if applied to Rome, from Roman Public Law. In both fields systematic and dogmatic teaching was traditional. But history was now beginning to pervade theology and jurisprudence. A new notion, both exacting and comprehensive, of human development left little space for mere descriptions of the past.

# What Is Ancient History? — Chapters 2-4

## Worldbreaking

WHERE WE WENT WRONG

One must always know the boundaries with great precision.

—FRIEDRICH AUGUST WOLF, ENCYCLOPÄDIE DER PHILOLOGIE1

WE DO NOT NORMALLY STUDY or teach ancient history in this manner. Why not? Had certain trends continued, we might have embraced a globalizing vision a long time ago. But as it happened, scholarship took a very different turn, leading us farther and farther away from inclusive, humanity-centered approaches. The world the worldbuilders made was broken up, smashed into pieces by their learned descendants.

The story of how this unfolded would fill a much longer book. It certainly deserves one. All I can do here is engage with traditions of scholarship that have become dominant in Western countries. I focus in particular on developments in intellectual and academic circles in eighteenth- and nineteenth-century Germany, which proved to be disproportionately influential. Just as contemporary universities around the globe are profoundly indebted to the German model of organizing research and teaching, so are the ways in which we have learned to deal with the remains of the ancient world.

In this chapter, I ask why the unprecedented expansion of connectivity on a planetary scale of the last few hundred years, and the equally unprecedented expansion and exchange of historical knowledge it made possible, did not foster a global perspective of the human past. I show how professionalization, nationalism, and racism interacted to create an academic landscape carved up into ever-smaller parcels that became separated by increasingly impermeable boundaries; and how a novel form of worship of ancient Greece and Rome provided a model of conceptual segregation that boosted these divisions while securing an exceptionally privileged position for those two cultures—so privileged in fact that they came to be equated with “ancient history” as such while broader perspectives fell by the wayside. I move back and forth between different levels of resolution—the study of Greece and Rome, of antiquity, and of history in general—all of which contributed to setting the course for our engagement with the ancient past.

49:Ernst Troeltsch, Der Historismus und seine Probleme, in Gesammelte Schriften (Tübingen: Mohr, 1922), III, 102.
59:参见Meinecke, Historismus, pp.1—10, and Troeltsch, Der Historismus und seine Probleme, pp.103—106, 372—375, 381。我在自己之前的文章中采纳了这样的区分，参见“Historicism” , The Oxford Handbook of Continental Philosophy, eds. Brian Leiter and Michael Rosen (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2007), pp.155—179。而基于文中陈述的理由，我现在拒斥这样的区分。梅尼克与特洛尔奇认为自然科学的解释模式只与实证主义相关，而实证主义直到19世纪40年代才成为一种有影响力的思想力量。例如，参见Troeltsch, Der Historismus und seine Probleme, pp.371—375。他们从而低估了赫尔德、默泽尔以及洪堡的“人的科学”计划的重要性。这种苏格兰启蒙运动的计划对德国思想家们的影响成为最近许多历史研究的主题。参见下文，第三章第2节以及第四章第6节。
61:历史主义经常被拿来与自然主义进行对比，好像对它的认同就在于主张历史知识方法是独特的，在类型上与自然科学的方法划清了界限。这正是梅尼克、特洛尔奇以及许多其他思想家的立场。然而，这一观点伴随着两大突出的问题。首先，事实上只有很少的历史主义者坚持历史的方法与自然科学的方法在本质上有所不同。这一普遍化观点在19世纪末德罗伊森与狄尔泰身上体现得尤为明显，他们坚信理解（Verstehen）这一方法明确地与自然主义相对。但是，如此单以方法论术语定义历史主义的方式严重限制了这些术语的外延。这使得历史主义传统分成两大部分—如果它们根本上能够合为一体的话。其次，历史主义生发自18世纪自然主义的程序，力求将牛顿物理学的方法和法则运用到历史之上，从而创建一门“关于人的科学”。那些历史主义传统的奠基者—克拉德尼乌斯、默泽尔、赫尔德和洪堡—实际上都是这种自然主义程序的捍卫者。历史主义的研究者—尤其是梅尼克—认同并且强调这些思想家的奠定性角色。因此如果我们要在历史主义与自然主义间进行严格区分的话，那么上述这些人都将被逐出历史主义传统之外，而极少数学者能够接受这种主张。既然历史主义传统与自然主义相对立是晚近的发展，仅仅在19世纪晚期由德罗伊森和狄尔泰发起，那么任何反自然主义的历史主义观念都是时代的误置。
63:参见Meinecke,Entstehung des Historismus, pp.155, 369, 595; and Troeltsch,Der Historismus und seine Probleme, pp.277—313。两人都强调了这些原则的活力论形而上学起源，无论它们是来自莱布尼茨（梅尼克的观点）还是谢林（特洛尔奇的观点）。这种形而上学确实在历史主义的早期阶段起到了重要的作用，而它在后来的阶段渐渐失去了核心地位；实际上存在着针对它的反动。整体论在狄尔泰、齐美尔与韦伯的著作中仍然显著，但它更多是方法论的而非形而上学的。
83:这是汉斯·格奥尔格·伽达默尔所犯的错误。他把一种粗陋的实证主义科学观念赋予历史主义传统。因为他认为，尽管历史主义传统试图发展出特有的历史方法，但它在接受客观与非个人知识理想方面仍然深受自然科学方法的影响。参见Wahrheit und Methode, in Gesammelte Werke (Tübingen: Mohr, 1990), I, 13, 235—236, 340, 344, 378—379。然而，只有兰克接近于拥护这样的理想，甚至他自己也不是在伽达默尔所想象的天真的意义上对其加以理解的。参见下文，第六章第4至6节。克拉德尼乌斯的视角主义对于历史主义传统具有重要的影响，它早已削弱了实证主义历史学观念。然而，伽达默尔从未接受克拉德尼乌斯的学说。参见下文，第一章第2节。考虑到德罗伊森、齐美尔与韦伯明确拒斥实证主义客观性观念，伽达默尔对历史主义的理解就显得尤为站不住脚。新康德主义者同样高度批判实证主义科学观念，尽管伽达默尔没有公正地看待他们。他关于新康德主义者的理解同样不合情理，指控他们怀有天真的“客观主义”。参见评论，“Vorwort zur 2. Auf lage” , in Gesammelte Werke II, 439，以及评论，“Hermeneutik und Historismus” , ibid, II, 388。不幸的是，伽达默尔继承了海德格尔对新康德主义者的反感而没有看得更远。
103:这是波普尔的历史主义概念。参见The Poverty of Historicism, p.3。参见Maurice Mandelbaum, History, Man & Reason (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins Press, 1971), p.42。这种历史主义的概念由梅尼克所发展，Meinecke, Die Entstehung des Historismus, pp.1—10; Troeltsch, Der Historismus und seine Probleme, pp.27—67, 102—110; Karl Mannheim, “Historismus” , Archiv für Sozialwissenschaft und Sozialpolitik 52 (1924), 1—60; and Georg Iggers, The German Conception of History (Middletown, CT: Wesleyan University Press, 1968), pp.3—42。这是伽达默尔的立场，Wahrheit und Methode, I, 203。
119:从历史主义的视角来看，启蒙运动的普遍问题除了来自它自身，还在于它虽自诩超越中世纪，却仍深陷中世纪思想遗产的窠臼。中世纪神学一直主张对社会、政治和道德价值的超验约定。虽然启蒙运动摆脱了宗教方面超验约定的困境，但它继续寻求更加世俗化的术语对此进行说明，无论这种超验约定是自然法、社会契约、普遍的人类理性抑或不变的人类本质。所有这些概念看上去保障了克服历史流变的有效性，以及超越了具体文化、政治和社会语境的约定性。所有启蒙运动的思想家（比如法国的哲学家、德国的启蒙者、英国的自由思想家）都想发现一些永恒的、普遍的阿基米德式支点，借此得以评判所有特定的社会、国家和文化。而历史主义深远内涵之一便是宣告这样的支点并不存在。
121:例如，参见Ernst Cassirer, The Philosophy of the Enlightenment (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1951), pp.197—233; Hans Peter Reill, The German Enlightenment and the Rise of Historicism (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1975), pp.2—3; Friedrich Jaeger and Jörn Rüsen, Geschichte des Historismus (Munich: Beck, 1992), pp.10—11; and Herbert Schnädelbach, Geschichtsphilosophie nach Hegel (Freiburg: Alber, 1974), pp.27—28。梅尼克批评者的指控在很大程度上是无的放矢。他们批判梅尼克的观点正是后者从未质疑过而且实际上竭尽全力试图论证的观点，即历史主义的根基在于启蒙的历史学。这甚至可以被认为是梅尼克《历史主义的兴起》的核心论题，它将历史主义的起源追溯到17、18世纪。
135:显而易见的是，19世纪代表性的历史主义者—兰克、德罗伊森、萨维尼、狄尔泰以及齐美尔—都自觉地、明白地拒斥自然法传统。这一传统在赫尔德、默泽尔和洪堡那里得到部分保留，他们使用自然法的术语，同时秉持着批判态度。所有历史主义传统的思想家坚持认为自然法教条非正当地将18世纪欧洲的道德价值普遍化为好像适用于所有时代和文化的价值。为了能了解文化或时代的价值，他们认为从内部出发的研究是必要的，应考察这些价值如何从历史和环境中发展出来。我们越是从历史的角度考察价值，我们越会注意到其目的与意义完全取决于特殊的语境以及它在社会历史整体中的确切地位。既然语境是独一无二、不可比较的，那么从中产生的价值同样如此；于是，我们无视社会、历史语境而试图普遍化每个人都应具备的价值将变得不再可能。
235:参见“Die Krise des Historismus” , Die neue Rundschau 33 (1922), 572—590。这篇文章是其大部头Der Historismus und seine Probleme (Tübingen: Mohr, 1922)的摘要。
251:例如，参见Bambach, Heidegger, Dilthey and the Crisis of Historicism (Ithaca: Cornell University Press, 1995), pp. 1—20; Iggers, German Conception of History, pp.128—129; and Meinecke, “Von der Krisis des Historismus” , in Werke IV, pp.200—201。

# 哥廷根学派

> 18 世纪哥廷根大学的语文学 seminar 传统，现代古典语文学职业训练的发源地。

## 概述

哥廷根大学建于 1737 年，以推进启蒙理想与新型学术为宗旨。1738 年，修辞学教授 Johann Matthias Gesner 在此设立语文学 seminar，这是古典语文学史上最早的此类机构。它以语文学为名，教学内容却远超希腊拉丁语，涵盖宗教、教育学、历史、地理、数学与自然科学，标志着从单纯的语言习得转向对古代文化内容与语境的理解。[[Heyne_Christian Gottlob|Christian Gottlob Heyne]] 长期主持该 seminar，把官方培养中学教师的委托实际改造成研究与学派再生产的工具：他既满足资助方的报告要求，又借此推进自己的研究议程、培养同道，累计培养三百余名学生。这一模式随后被校友和模仿者复制到各地。

## 关键人物 / 相关著作

- [[Heyne_Christian Gottlob|Heyne]] — seminar 的实际形塑者，其百科全书式概览讲座吸引大量校内外听众
- [[Wolf_Friedrich August|Friedrich August Wolf]]、[[Humboldt_Wilhelm von|Wilhelm von Humboldt]] — 均曾受教于 Heyne，后来提出更激进的学科纲领
- Gatterer 与 Schlözer — 同期在哥廷根探索普遍史与世界史，其路向后被专业化的古典研究挤占

## 在学科史中的位置

Most 将现代古典语文学方法与制度从哥廷根 seminar 出发、经 Wolf 的课程、再到柏林大学与人文中学的传播，视为 18–19 世纪科学现代化中最壮观的过程之一。哥廷根因此既是 [[柏林大学]] 语文学传统的直接前身，也是 [[Altertumswissenschaft]] 纲领的制度土壤。

## 出处
- [[学术史文献/Scheidel_2025_什么是古代史（第2-4章）|Scheidel 2025]] 第 2 章：1737 年建校、1738 年 Gesner 设 seminar、Heyne 主持 seminar 及三百余名毕业生
- [[学术史文献/Most_2002_Disciplining Classics（前言）|Most 2002]] 前言：从哥廷根 seminar 经 Wolf 到柏林大学的传播叙事

## 待探索
- 哥廷根语文学 seminar 与 Gatterer、Schlözer 普遍史尝试之间的制度与人事关系
- Gesner 设立 seminar 的具体章程与课程内容

# 柏林大学

> 1810 年建立的普鲁士大学，古典语文学与古代学在 19 世纪的学科中枢。

## 概述

[[Humboldt_Wilhelm von|Wilhelm von Humboldt]] 在 19 世纪初深度参与了柏林大学的建立与普鲁士教育制度改革，该校后来以他命名。[[Wolf_Friedrich August|Friedrich August Wolf]] 自 1795 年起反复讲授"语文学百科全书"，先在哈勒、后到柏林，其 seminar 与讲义成为学科模板。他最有名的学生 [[Boeckh_August|August Böckh]] 在柏林培养了几代学者，1809 至 1865 年间讲授同名"语文学百科全书"达二十六次，坚持有机整体论与历史语境，同时仍奉语言能力为开启古代的"主要钥匙"。

## 关键人物 / 相关著作

- [[Boeckh_August|August Böckh]] — Wolf 学说的继承者与柏林语文学的核心教师
- [[Mommsen_Theodor|Theodor Mommsen]] — 罗马古代史最著名的实践者，却并不承认"古代史"是一门有意义的学科（详见 [[Römische Geschichte]]）
- [[Wilamowitz-Moellendorff_Ulrich von|Ulrich von Wilamowitz-Moellendorff]]、[[Meyer_Eduard|Eduard Meyer]] — 1900 年前后主导柏林，分别主张重建统一的古代学研究所与拒绝古代学合并

## 在学科史中的位置

Scheidel 指出，正如 18 世纪末的哥廷根，1900 年前后的柏林同样成为把史学家拉向相反方向的孵化器。Wilamowitz 力图建立统辖全部希腊罗马事务的单一研究所，但其时古代史与考古学已高度独立，[[Altertumswissenschaft]] 的统一理想名存实亡。

## 出处
- [[学术史文献/Scheidel_2025_什么是古代史（第2-4章）|Scheidel 2025]] 第 2 章：Humboldt 与柏林大学、Böckh 二十六次讲座、Mommsen 与古代史教席、1900 年前后 Wilamowitz 与 Meyer 的对立

## 待探索
- 1810 年建校章程中语文学与古代学的具体建制安排
- Wilamowitz 1907 年合并研究所的组织细节

# Warburg图书馆

> Aby Warburg 在汉堡建立的文化科学图书馆（Kulturwissenschaftliche Bibliothek Warburg），1933 年迁往伦敦。

## 概述

该馆由艺术史家与文化史家 [[Warburg_Aby|Aby Warburg]] 创建，以"文化科学"（Kulturwissenschaft）为名，其藏书按"记忆—取向—表达"一类问题域而非学科分类编排，意在让图像、文字与仪式材料在同一问题下相互照亮。这一取向对 20 世纪的图像学与古代宗教研究影响深远，[[Momigliano_Arnaldo|Momigliano]] 论古代史与古物学家的名文即与该馆关系密切：该文初稿 1949 年 1 月在 Warburg Institute 宣读，后刊于 *Journal of the Warburg and Courtauld Institutes* 第 13 卷（1950）。

## 关键人物 / 相关著作

- [[Warburg_Aby|Aby Warburg]] — 创始人，图像学与"古代之来世"（Nachleben der Antike）研究的开创者
- [[Momigliano_Arnaldo|Momigliano]] — 《古代史与古物学家》初稿在该馆宣读，并发表在该馆所办刊物上
- [[Grafton_Anthony|Anthony Grafton]] — 后续在该馆学术脉络中研究古物学与学术史

## 在学科史中的位置

Warburg 图书馆所代表的跨学科"文化科学"路线，与德国式 [[Altertumswissenschaft]] 的语文学中心主义形成对照：前者以问题统摄材料，后者以语言文献为等级序列之首。1933 年迁往伦敦，使这一德国学术传统在英国得以延续，并成为英语世界古典学与艺术史交叉研究的重要机构。

## 出处
- [[学术史文献/Momigliano_1950_Ancient History and the Antiquarian|Momigliano 1950]] 注释：该文初稿 1949 年 1 月在 Warburg Institute 宣读；出处信息为 *Journal of the Warburg and Courtauld Institutes*, Vol. 13, No. 3/4 (1950)

## 待探索
- Warburg 图书馆在汉堡的确切建馆年份与最初藏书规模
- 1933 年迁馆的具体经过，及其与汉堡大学的关系

# 德国历史主义

> 18 世纪中叶至 20 世纪初的德国思想传统，主张人类世界的一切皆为历史所造就。

## 概述

按 Beiser 的界定，经典历史主义传统在德国肇始于 18 世纪中叶的 [[Chladenius_Johann Martin|Chladenius]]，终结于 20 世纪初的 [[Weber_Max|Max Weber]]。其核心主张是：文化、价值、制度、实践乃至理性都由历史造就，没有任何东西具有永恒形式、固定本质或超历史的恒常认同——人类事物中不存在"永恒实质"与"变化偶然"的二分。因此凡试图把特定价值普遍化为适用于全人类或普遍理性的做法，都被视为种族中心主义的幻象。这一传统自觉地拒斥自然法，视其非正当地将 18 世纪欧洲价值冒充为普遍价值。

## 关键人物 / 相关著作

- 奠基者：[[Chladenius_Johann Martin|Chladenius]]、[[Moeser_Justus|Möser]]、[[Herder_Johann Gottfried|Herder]]、[[Humboldt_Wilhelm von|Humboldt]]
- 鼎盛期代表：[[Ranke_Leopold von|Ranke]]、[[Droysen_Johann Gustav|Droysen]]、[[Dilthey_Wilhelm|Dilthey]]、[[Simmel_Georg|Simmel]]、[[Troeltsch_Ernst|Troeltsch]]、[[Meinecke_Friedrich|Meinecke]]
- [[Lamprecht_Karl|Karl Lamprecht]] — 其 1890 年代的方法论挑战引发 [[兰普雷希特之争]]

## 在学科史中的位置

Beiser 在 [[历史主义的兴起|Meinecke《历史主义的兴起》]] 的基础上重述该传统，并逐一检讨关于"历史主义危机"的五种说法（相对主义与虚无主义、[[Nietzsche_Friedrich|Nietzsche]] 的批判、[[兰普雷希特之争]]、一战对进步信念的摧毁、客观知识与历史决定之间的内部矛盾）。他的结论是：历史主义并非凄惨落败，而是达成"让史学成为一门科学"的原初目标后自然式微，其影响至今仍在。术语概念另有 [[Historismus]] 一条。

## 出处
- [[学术史文献/Beiser_2011_德国历史主义传统（前言·导论）|Beiser 2011]] 前言·导论：传统的起讫（Chladenius 至 Weber）、核心主张、五条危机说及其评价

## 待探索
- Beiser 所批评的 Meinecke"概念图式简单化"具体指什么
- 历史主义与 [[Altertumswissenschaft]] 在制度上的重合程度

# Altertumswissenschaft

> "古代学"，由 [[Wolf_Friedrich August|F. A. Wolf]] 提出的德国式古典研究学科纲领。

## 概述

Scheidel 指出该词难以译成英文："Science of Antiquity"过于偏硬科学，"Antiquityknowledgecraft"才近似其意涵，因此他径用德文原词。Wolf 起初用"Alte Litteratur"（古代文献）指同一议程，直到为 [[Winckelmann_Johann Joachim|Winckelmann]] 所写的颂词中才让"Altertumswissenschaft"一词登场，呼吁学科"整体"成形。该纲领一方面宣称包罗万象，一方面把语言与文献置于最高等级：Wolf 把学科分为多达二十四个分支，从语法到艺术与地理研究，但其"基础性原则"仍是语言文学优先于艺术与考古。其主题实为"GreeceandRome"——一个把希腊与罗马熔为一体的、封闭于自身的世界。

## 关键人物 / 相关著作

- [[Wolf_Friedrich August|Wolf]]、[[Boeckh_August|Böckh]] — 纲领的提出者与继承者，后者在柏林继续讲授"语文学百科全书"
- [[Wilamowitz-Moellendorff_Ulrich von|Wilamowitz]] — 在柏林力图重建统一研究所
- [[Meyer_Eduard|Eduard Meyer]] — 明确拒斥该词，认为把史学与语文学合并为"古代学"不合理且有害

## 在学科史中的位置

该纲领自 19 世纪起逐步碎裂：古典考古学与古代史教席分别于 1840、1860 年代出现，19 世纪末希腊语文学与拉丁语文学分家，20 世纪初拜占庭学与中世纪拉丁语获得教席。Wilamowitz 1900 年已承认"古代作为统一体与理想已经消失"。Scheidel 认为，欧洲大陆这套模式的消失并未自动带来更包容的古代研究，而其英美孪生子即 Classics。

## 出处
- [[学术史文献/Scheidel_2025_什么是古代史（第2-4章）|Scheidel 2025]] 第 2 章：术语的不可译性、Wolf 的二十四个分支、"语言文学优先"的原则、19 世纪的分科与 Wilamowitz、Meyer 的反对

## 待探索
- Wolf 1807 年纲要（*Darstellung der Alterthums-Wissenschaft*）的完整目录结构
- "GreeceandRome"这一构造在英美 Classics 中的对应形态

# Historismus

> "历史主义"概念及其语义流变，Beiser 导论的核心议题之一。

## 概述

Beiser 强调任何定义此词的尝试都会立即遭遇障碍：它蕴含太多甚至相互冲突的意义。对一些人（如 Popper 所贬斥的 historicism）它指试图确定历史普遍法则；对另一些人（如 [[Meinecke_Friedrich|Meinecke]]）其意义恰好相反，标志对这些法则的拒斥、对历史上独特单一事件与个性的把握。他采纳 [[Troeltsch_Ernst|Troeltsch]] 的定义，即剥离否定含义后，"历史主义"意味着"我们有关人类及其文化与价值的所有思考的根本上的历史化"。

## 关键人物 / 相关著作

- [[Troeltsch_Ernst|Troeltsch]] — 首位赋予该词现代含义者（*Der Historismus und seine Probleme*）
- [[Meinecke_Friedrich|Meinecke]] — 在"拒斥普遍法则"的意义上使用该词（详见 [[历史主义的兴起]]）
- [[Chladenius_Johann Martin|Chladenius]]、[[Moeser_Justus|Möser]]、[[Herder_Johann Gottfried|Herder]]、[[Humboldt_Wilhelm von|Humboldt]] — Beiser 认定的奠基者
- [[Droysen_Johann Gustav|Droysen]]、[[Dilthey_Wilhelm|Dilthey]] — 反自然主义历史观的倡导者

## 在学科史中的位置

Beiser 反对把历史主义简单等同于"历史方法区别于自然科学方法"的反自然主义立场。他指出，事实上极少历史主义者坚持二者本质不同；19 世纪末才由 Droysen 与 Dilthey 以"理解"（Verstehen）为旗号发起的反自然主义，属于晚近发展。反之，该传统恰恰生发自 18 世纪的自然主义程序——力图把牛顿式方法用于历史，建立"关于人的科学"。若严格以反自然主义界定历史主义，则其奠基者都将被逐出传统之外。作为思潮/学派者另见 [[德国历史主义]]。

## 出处
- [[学术史文献/Beiser_2011_德国历史主义传统（前言·导论）|Beiser 2011]] 前言·导论：词的歧义（Popper 与 Meinecke 两种用法）、Troeltsch 的现代定义、对反自然主义式定义的批评

## 待探索
- Historismus 一词的德语词源与 19 世纪用法史（Beiser 注中列举 Rothacker 等研究）
- 与 Historizismus 一词的区分

# Foundational History

> Scheidel 提出的"基础史/奠基史"概念：把"古代史"重构为全人类共享的奠基史。

## 概述

Scheidel 的核心主张是：过去二百五十年间，学术理念与实践使人越来越难以探索、理解并传播我们共享的"奠基史"（foundational history）。吊诡之处在于，这一趋势恰与古文字与古语言的破译、考古田野工作的兴起同步——后者本应首次使这样一部奠基史成为可能。在他笔下，奠基史指"最大隔绝"阶段的历史：全新世已将美洲与亚非欧隔断，而现代大西洋交流尚未开始。因此它虽然规模上是全球的，却并不以"关联性"为定义标准，这使它区别于以 connectivity 为核心的 global history，也更依赖比较史与世界史方法。

## 关键人物 / 相关著作

- 概念由 Scheidel 提出，作为对 [[Altertumswissenschaft]] 与英美 Classics 之局限的诊断与替代方案
- [[Herder_Johann Gottfried|Herder]]、[[Winckelmann_Johann Joachim|Winckelmann]] — 其希腊中心论与"东方模式"之争被引为对照
- 书中设专节"Who Is Afraid of Foundational History?"检讨学术体制的抵制

## 在学科史中的位置

Scheidel 认为，只要 [[Altertumswissenschaft]] 式的希腊罗马排他性仍在，真正的奠基史便难以展开；他主张"把古代史重构为奠基史"是让古代研究在当下重新获得相关性的关键。他甚至断言，全球古代史若被理解为奠基史，就是"我们"——无论何人、身处何地——的古代史。

## 出处
- [[学术史文献/Scheidel_2025_什么是古代史（第2-4章）|Scheidel 2025]] 第 2 章开篇（"世界断裂"）与"Who Is Afraid of Foundational History?"一节；尤见论 250 年趋势、奠基史的时间范围（全新世之后、大西洋交流之前）与比较/世界史方法

## 待探索
- 该概念与 Sebastian Conrad 全球史论述的关系
- Scheidel 书第 1 章对"奠基史"的完整定义与分卷规划

# 兰普雷希特之争

> 1890 年代围绕 Karl Lamprecht《德国史》展开的德国史学方法论之争（Methodenstreit）。

## 概述

Beiser 将其列为解释"历史主义危机"的第三种理论。[[Lamprecht_Karl|Karl Lamprecht]] 自 1891 年起出版《德国史》（至 1909 年），主张史学应像自然科学那样确定普遍的因果律，并据此为方法论辩护。这一主张向威廉时代最重要的历史学家发起挑战，被卷入者包括 [[Meinecke_Friedrich|Friedrich Meinecke]] 以及 Max Delbrück、Otto Hintze、Max Lenz、Hermann Oncken、Georg von Below，而这些人皆成长于兰克学派传统之内。争论主要在 Lamprecht 与 von Below 之间展开，史称"兰普雷希特之争"。据说这场辩论使历史主义者对自身方法论失去了信心。

## 关键人物 / 相关著作

- [[Lamprecht_Karl|Karl Lamprecht]] — 《德国史》，主张基于自然科学的历史观
- [[Meinecke_Friedrich|Meinecke]] — 应战者之一，其 [[历史主义的兴起]] 展现了对该传统更精细的辩护
- Max Delbrück、Otto Hintze、Max Lenz、Hermann Oncken、Georg von Below — 兰克学派内的论战参与者

## 在学科史中的位置

Beiser 本人并不认为这场论战足以解释历史主义的消逝。他指出五种危机说共同的问题是：它们都预设历史主义因深层悲剧性缺陷而衰落，然而思想家们对所谓缺陷从未达成一致，且思想运动很少仅因理论难点而偃旗息鼓。他给出的替代解释是：历史主义完成了让史学成为独立科学专业的原初任务，故不再需要以运动形态存在。

## 出处
- [[学术史文献/Beiser_2011_德国历史主义传统（前言·导论）|Beiser 2011]] 前言·导论：危机说之三（Lamprecht《德国史》1891–1909、论战参与者名单、Methodenstreit）；及对该说的评价

## 待探索
- 论战的具体时间线与主要文本（Lamprecht 与 von Below 的交锋）
- 该争论对德国经济史与文化史方法的影响

# Prolegomena ad Homerum

> [[Wolf_Friedrich August|F. A. Wolf]]《荷马绪论》（1795），近代语文学的开端之作。

## 概述

Scheidel 称此书为 Wolf 的"杰作"（masterpiece），并把它放在两条线索的交汇处。其一是学科史线索：Wolf 1787 年在哈勒创办了模仿哥廷根的语文学 seminar，1795 年起又反复讲授"语文学百科全书"，而《绪论》正是这一研究取向的典范成果。其二是自我否定的线索：Scheidel 特别指出，Wolf 后来为强化"GreeceandRome"的排他性模板，不得不排斥比较性问题——这实际上是对他本人在《绪论》中所作的希腊与圣经语文学比较研究的隐晦否定，"学科化要求自我规训"。

## 关键人物 / 相关著作

- [[Wolf_Friedrich August|F. A. Wolf]] — 作者，哈勒 seminar 创办者、[[Altertumswissenschaft]] 纲领的提出者
- 与 [[Heyne_Christian Gottlob|Heyne]] 的哥廷根语文学传统相关，Wolf 为该传统的继承与激进化者

## 在学科史中的位置

该书把《伊利亚特》《奥德赛》并非一人一时写定、而系口传材料后期编集的论断推向前台，使"荷马问题"成为近代语文学的起点，也让文本考订与历史批判成为学科方法核心。它与 [[Altertumswissenschaft]] 的纲领互为表里：既确立了语文学的方法尊严，又暴露出该纲领在比较视野上的自我封闭。

## 出处
- [[学术史文献/Scheidel_2025_什么是古代史（第2-4章）|Scheidel 2025]] 第 2 章：Wolf 1787 年在哈勒办 seminar；《荷马绪论》1795 年；Wolf 排拒比较研究实为对其自身比较语文学工作的否定

## 待探索
- Wolf 关于荷马史诗编集与口传的具体论证（Peisistratus 编集说）及其后世争议
- 《绪论》英译与接受史

# 历史主义的兴起

> [[Meinecke_Friedrich|Meinecke]]《Die Entstehung des Historismus》(1936)，Beiser 的主要对话对象。

## 概述

Meinecke 在 1936 年为该书所写的序言中怀旧地断言，历史主义"是西方思潮所经历的最伟大的思想革命之一"。其宏大志向是追踪德国历史主义的起源：上起 17 世纪末这一传统的开端，下迄以 [[Ranke_Leopold von|Ranke]] 为代表的传统顶峰。该书的核心论题是把历史主义的根基追溯到启蒙史学，即 17、18 世纪的宗教与思想语境之中。

## 关键人物 / 相关著作

- [[Meinecke_Friedrich|Meinecke]] — 作者；另有《历史主义的危机》等文，并参与 [[兰普雷希特之争]]
- [[Ranke_Leopold von|Ranke]] — 书中传统的顶峰
- [[Troeltsch_Ernst|Troeltsch]] — 与 Meinecke 共同界定 [[Historismus]] 的现代含义
- Beiser 的著作以该书为"主要先例与典范"，但试图据后续研究重述整个故事

## 在学科史中的位置

Beiser 既承认其文本分析的洞察力与历史视角的深度广度，也指出严重缺陷：Meinecke 忽视了关键人物（如 [[Moeser_Justus|Möser]]、[[Herder_Johann Gottfried|Herder]]、[[Humboldt_Wilhelm von|Humboldt]] 的"人的科学"计划被低估），阐释常误置时代，概念图式则具误导性与简单化特征；其追踪在五百页后仍未超越歌德。针对"Meinecke 把历史主义根基归入启蒙"的批评，Beiser 反驳说这恰恰是 Meinecke 竭力论证的核心论题，指控属无的放矢。

## 出处
- [[学术史文献/Beiser_2011_德国历史主义传统（前言·导论）|Beiser 2011]] 前言·导论：Meinecke 1936 年序言引文、该书起讫与核心论题、Beiser 对其缺陷的批评（含注 37 所引 Werke III 版本信息）

## 待探索
- Meinecke 概念图式"误导性与简单化"的具体所指
- 该书对 Goethe 的处理为何使其未能抵达 Ranke

# Römische Geschichte

> [[Mommsen_Theodor|Theodor Mommsen]]《罗马史》，兼及其学术与政治的交织。

## 概述

在 Scheidel 的叙述中，Mommsen 是希腊罗马"古代史"最著名的实践者，然而他本人并不承认"古代史"是一门有意义的学术领域。这一暧昧恰好反映该领域的定位困境：1869 至 1904 年间设立的二十一个古代史教席，有的挂靠在 [[Altertumswissenschaft]] 之下，有的则不然，唯一把它们统合起来的是对希腊罗马的固执坚守与对其它一切的排斥。Mommsen 的《罗马史》正是这一时期的代表成就，其史料批判与碑铭学功夫承接 [[Niebuhr_Barthold Georg|Niebuhr]] 把 Wolf 语文学方法施用于罗马史的路向。

## 关键人物 / 相关著作

- [[Mommsen_Theodor|Mommsen]] — 作者，罗马史与拉丁碑铭学（*Corpus Inscriptionum Latinarum*）的奠基者
- [[Niebuhr_Barthold Georg|Niebuhr]] — 以语文学方法改造罗马史研究的先驱

## 在学科史中的位置

Mommsen 兼为自由派政治家，任普鲁士众议院与帝国议会议员，1851 年因 1848 年革命时期的政治活动被撤去莱比锡教职，1858 年赴柏林就任特设的研究教席；1902 年以《罗马史》获诺贝尔文学奖。其书止于前三卷（1854–1856）与记述行省的第五卷（1885），记述帝政的第四卷始终未写出。这一"未完成"与他的政治关怀、以及他对古代史学科定位的怀疑，共同构成理解该书的线索。

## 出处
- [[学术史文献/Scheidel_2025_什么是古代史（第2-4章）|Scheidel 2025]] 第 2 章：Mommsen 为"古代史"最著名实践者却不视其为有意义的学科、1869–1904 年的二十一个教席、Niebuhr 以 Wolf 语文学方法改造罗马史

## 待探索
- "学术政治"一面：Mommsen 的政治生涯与其史学写作的具体关联（如对恺撒的评价与自由主义史观）
- 第四卷未完成的根本原因及其在研究中引起的争论

# Geschichte des Altertums

> [[Meyer_Eduard|Eduard Meyer]]《古代史》，以整体古代史反对语文学式的古代学。

## 概述

Eduard Meyer 是 1900 年前后与 [[Wilamowitz-Moellendorff_Ulrich von|Wilamowitz]] 并列的柏林学人，Scheidel 视二人为当时把古典研究拉向相反方向的代表。Meyer 的多卷本《古代史》把埃及与西亚纳入同一叙事，其方法论立场则明确反对 Wolf 式的学科构想：他断言，就古代研究而言，"把两者合并、归入'[[Altertumswissenschaft]]'名下，是不合理且令人困惑的，并且已对古代史的处理造成相当损害"——这种合并人为地促进了本属一体的东西被切割，也助长了专门化。他坚持古代史"只能是单一普遍史的一部分"。

## 关键人物 / 相关著作

- [[Meyer_Eduard|Eduard Meyer]] — 作者，柏林古代史教授
- [[Wilamowitz-Moellendorff_Ulrich von|Wilamowitz]] — 其柏林研究所重组正是 Meyer 批评的直接对象
- [[Niebuhr_Barthold Georg|Niebuhr]]、[[Mommsen_Theodor|Mommsen]] — 德国古代史写作的前驱（另见 [[Römische Geschichte]]）

## 在学科史中的位置

Meyer 试图把"古代史"向古代埃及与西亚开放，但 Scheidel 指出这一努力遇到三重障碍：胜任所需的博学几乎只可能属于通才；时代精神正把民族主义推向空前高度；以及 Meyer 本人语言细节功底受到 Wilamowitz 的公开质疑。这一路向终未成功，德国境内维护统一 Altertumswissenschaft 与开放古代史的努力双双落空。

## 出处
- [[学术史文献/Scheidel_2025_什么是古代史（第2-4章）|Scheidel 2025]] 第 2 章：1900 年前后柏林 Wilamowitz 与 Meyer 的对立、Meyer 拒绝 Altertumswissenschaft 合并的引文、其方案面临的三重障碍

## 待探索
- 《古代史》各卷的确切出版年份与覆盖范围
- Meyer 与 Wilamowitz 在柏林研究所改组中的具体冲突经过

8	# 德国历史主义
9	
10	> 18 世纪中叶至 20 世纪初的德国思想传统，主张人类世界的一切皆为历史所造就。
11	
12	## 概述
13	
14	按 Beiser 的界定，经典历史主义传统在德国肇始于 18 世纪中叶的 [[Chladenius_Johann Martin|Chladenius]]，终结于 20 世纪初的 [[Weber_Max|Max Weber]]。其核心主张是：文化、价值、制度、实践乃至理性都由历史造就，没有任何东西具有永恒形式、固定本质或超历史的恒常认同——人类事物中不存在"永恒实质"与"变化偶然"的二分。因此凡试图把特定价值普遍化为适用于全人类或普遍理性的做法，都被视为种族中心主义的幻象。这一传统自觉地拒斥自然法，视其非正当地将 18 世纪欧洲价值冒充为普遍价值。
15	
16	## 关键人物 / 相关著作
17	
18	- 奠基者：[[Chladenius_Johann Martin|Chladenius]]、[[Moeser_Justus|Möser]]、[[Herder_Johann Gottfried|Herder]]、[[Humboldt_Wilhelm von|Humboldt]]
19	- 鼎盛期代表：[[Ranke_Leopold von|Ranke]]、[[Droysen_Johann Gustav|Droysen]]、[[Dilthey_Wilhelm|Dilthey]]、[[Simmel_Georg|Simmel]]、[[Troeltsch_Ernst|Troeltsch]]、[[Meinecke_Friedrich|Meinecke]]
20	- [[Lamprecht_Karl|Karl Lamprecht]] — 其 1890 年代的方法论挑战引发 [[兰普雷希特之争]]
21	
22	## 在学科史中的位置
23	
24	Beiser 在 [[历史主义的兴起|Meinecke《历史主义的兴起》]] 的基础上重述该传统，并逐一检讨关于"历史主义危机"的五种说法（相对主义与虚无主义、[[Nietzsche_Friedrich|Nietzsche]] 的批判、[[兰普雷希特之争]]、一战对进步信念的摧毁、客观知识与历史决定之间的内部矛盾）。他的结论是：历史主义并非凄惨落败，而是达成"让史学成为一门科学"的原初目标后自然式微，其影响至今仍在。术语概念另有 [[Historismus]] 一条。
